reviews.review_text:
There is something really magical about ‘The Clockmaker’s Daughter’. It is like a whimsical fairytale with the most beautiful score but underneath that lies a story with so much heart and emotional depth. It is a show that asks important questions about belonging and acceptance. Avonmore Musical Society embraced all of that beautifully in their production at St Mary’s Hall, Arklow. The story was told with imagination, sincerity and affection, giving us a wonderfully warm night at the theatre. It had everything that is good about amateur musical theatre, with its strong emphasis on community, imagination, talent and, above all else, real heart.

Great effort had gone into the front of house experience. The foyer was very nicely decorated, continuing the steampunk aesthetic of the production with visible cogs front of house. There was a warm and welcoming atmosphere from the moment we arrived. Front of house staff were friendly, approachable and clearly proud of the production they were presenting. It all contributed nicely to the evening and set a lovely tone for what was to follow on stage.

Amy Penston Hendley directed the production with a confident and very thoughtful hand. It was clear that she understood the heart of the piece. Underneath the fantasy and fairytale elements of ‘The Clockmaker’s Daughter’ lies a story about fear of difference and the speed with which ordinary people can be swept up in mob mentality. Those themes, so relevant in today’s world, came across strongly. Ms. Penston Hendley found a lovely balance between the story’s comedy and emotion. There was great attention to narrative detail throughout. Scene transitions flowed very smoothly and contributed to the show’s excellent pace. There were many beautifully realised moments throughout the show. ‘Where You’ll Be’ was stunning both visually and emotionally, with beautifully simple staging, gorgeous lighting and superb vocals capturing the storybook quality of the piece. There were also lovely smaller details throughout the show. Abraham pausing to touch the workshop door after Will had been shot was a beautiful directorial choice, saying so much in one simple action. Likewise, the moment of Will leaving a flower beside Constance’s statue had genuine emotional sincerity. Overall, this was superb work with tremendous heart and skill in what is a deceptively difficult show to direct well.

Martina Murphy’s choreography was very successful throughout. Ms. Murphy’s work was all about telling the story and contributed hugely to the building of character, atmosphere and emotion. There was a lovely sense of energy and optimism in ‘The Turning of the Key’, with appropriate, natural movement giving the village of Spindlewood great life and personality. There was particularly lovely work in ‘A Modest Modiste’. The seamstresses’ choreography using the measuring tapes had a nice softness and elegance to it and the final picture was especially beautiful. ‘Raise a Glass’ was one of the standout choreographic sequences of the evening. The celebratory dancing was joyful and infectious, with excellent high-energy movement. I really admired the dramatic movement used during ‘Fear and Whispers’. The broken clockwork-inspired physicality from the ensemble worked brilliantly in reflecting the growing fear, suspicion and mob mentality spreading through the town. Excellent storytelling through choreography.

Conor McCarthy did stunning work as musical director, bringing Michael Webborn and Daniel Finn’s gorgeous score to life with great care and sensitivity, ably assisted throughout by chorus mistress Jennifer Lee. Principal singing throughout was consistently excellent. What stood out most, however, was the quality of the ensemble and choral singing. From the opening moments of ‘The Turning of the Key’, the chorus produced a wonderfully full and confident sound with their exceptional harmonies. ‘Raise a Glass’ was musically outstanding. The power and energy of the ensemble vocals was stunning, adding hugely to what was one of the show’s most memorable sequences. The orchestra was excellent and complemented the vocals beautifully. Overall, an exceptionally high musical standard throughout.

Áine Kinch gave a superb performance as Constance, capturing both the innocence and emotional complexity of the character with great sensitivity throughout. There was something truly captivating about this performance. Ms. Kinch embraced Constance’s childlike curiosity and naivety so well and also allowed her humanity to emerge little by little as the story unfolded. Vocally, she was outstanding. Her performance of ‘Impossible’ was stunning, delivered with tremendous control and emotional honesty. It was one of those pin-drop moments where the audience was completely drawn into the performance. ‘A Story of My Own’ was another lovely moment, with Ms. Kinch beautifully capturing Constance’s growing self-awareness and emotional awakening. Dramatically, she was so impressive. Ms. Kinch paid great attention to the physicality of the role. Her precise posture and movement made her very believable as someone who was not quite fully human. Excellent work all round from Ms. Kinch.

Daniel Furlong was outstanding in the dual role of Storyteller and Will, giving a performance which was full of warmth, sincerity and emotion throughout. Mr. Furlong had an easy charm and a wonderfully engaging presence. There was something incredibly natural about his performance and he was utterly believable from beginning to end. As Storyteller, he established an immediate rapport with the audience, with great confidence and ease. As Will, his understanding of dialogue and pace was exceptional. His developing relationship with Constance was beautifully handled. His singing was equally exceptional. Vocals were expressive and effortless, always telling the story. He impressed greatly in ‘If You Could See My Heart’, with excellent vocal technique and a great understanding of the lyrics, delivered with genuine emotion. An exceptional performance from a hugely talented performer.

Andrew Docherty gave a superb portrayal of the clockmaker, Abraham. Abraham is such a complex character. He is a grieving father and a man desperately trying to hold on to something he has lost. He has so much love but also fear, guilt and sadness. It is a role that can easily become overly stern or distant but I thought that Mr. Docherty found the humanity in Abraham beautifully. He brought wonderful sympathy to the role, as we saw his flaws and fears but still we remained emotionally invested in his story. He sang very well throughout. ‘You Are Still Here’ had great feeling and sincerity, with a warm and expressive baritone and excellent acting through song.

Emily Davis was very strong as Amelia Kelly, bringing great intelligence and emotional understanding to the role. There was a real sense of thought behind every interaction. As an actress, she was consistently impressive. Ms. Davis brought a lovely, natural quality to her performance. Vocally, she was equally strong. ‘Raise a Glass’ showed the quality of her voice beautifully. Overall, a very thoughtful portrayal throughout.

Joanne Logue delivered an excellent performance as Ma Riley, full of energy, personality and presence. As the central antagonist she embodied the darker themes of the show but also provided much of the show’s humour and larger-than-life characterisation. Striking the right balance between the two is not easy but Ms. Logue handled it extremely well. Characterisation was consistently strong throughout. She had excellent stage presence and a wonderful physicality. Comedy was very well handled too, creating a figure who was entertaining while still allowing us to see the darker, more spiteful side of the character as the story progressed. That transition into the more unpleasant and dangerous Ma Riley was very convincingly played by Ms. Logue.

Kevin Macken was very impressive as Henry Glynn, creating one of the most memorable supporting characters of the show. What impressed me most was the intelligence behind Mr. Macken’s performance. His acting was so natural and believable throughout. His comic timing was excellent. Small moments, such as his attempts to retrieve the watch or his realisation that Amelia’s dress would not be ready until Monday, were played with great understanding of the humour. A really memorable supporting performance, played with charm and intelligence throughout.

Seán Hendley brought great warmth and a light comic touch to his portrayal of Mayor Glynn. Mr. Hendley’s strength as a character actor showed throughout in the confidence and detail of his performance. He found lots of humour in the role but in a most natural way, never pushing the comedy, ensuring that Mayor Glynn was authentic and believable. Overall, wonderful work throughout from Mr Hendley, in a portrayal that was full of lovely character detail.

The very committed ensemble work throughout was highly impressive and a huge part of why the show worked so successfully. There was constant life and character within the community of Spindlewood and a lot of effort had clearly gone into developing this. The seamstresses in particular were excellent throughout. Orlagh Sunderland as Rhiannon, Zoe Cummins as Mary, Izabela Wong as Jane, Molly-Rose Smith as Lucille, Niamh Harper as Moll, Erin Connolly as Cara and Amber Doyle as Sue worked beautifully together both during ‘A Modest Modiste’. Their singing was wonderfully blended, while their movement and interactions were well-rehearsed and in tune with the narrative. Strong support also came from Tomás Byrne as John, Eoghan Kinsella as Sam, Fionn Vigors as Ted, Gary Joyce as Jim, Callum Murray as Dave and Elaine McMahon Dossett as Mab, all of whom contributed greatly to Spindlewood’s sense of community. Fiona Redmond also made a very strong impression in her cameo appearance as Mrs. Reece. Musically, the ensemble was outstanding. Their singing was excellent and it was obvious that an enormous amount of rehearsal had gone into the choral work.

Barry Ryan and his crew did absolutely outstanding work. ‘The Clockmaker’s Daughter’ can be a challenging show, with its constant shifts between interior and exterior locations and its fast transitions. Thanks to an exceptionally well-rehearsed crew, the entire operation ran with remarkable smoothness and precision. The choice to costume crew was a clever one, ensuring that we were never pulled out of the fairytale world of Spindlewood during transitions. The trucks themselves were moved incredibly smoothly and meant that the whole production flowed with remarkable fluidity. The result was stage management of an exceptionally high standard throughout.

Set design was quite beautiful and captured the magical, storybook quality of ‘The Clockmaker’s Daughter’ wonderfully well. I loved the steampunk aesthetic, with oversized cogs and clockwork imagery creating a most atmospheric playing space. The trucks for Abraham’s workshop and Ma Riley’s shop were very impressive. Each had lovely detail and character. The bridge was another gorgeous piece of design, which reinforced the fairytale feel of the production. Overall, it was a set which facilitated the storytelling beautifully, full of atmosphere and great detail. A credit to all involved.

The lighting design was, at its best, absolutely stunning. It was often atmospheric and visually beautiful, contributing greatly to the magical, storybook feel of the production. There were so many times where lighting, set, haze and performance came together in really breathtaking ways, creating some stunning stage pictures. ‘A Story of My Own’ was particularly well handled, with the moving light tracking Constance with impressive precision and subtle changes in colour beautifully enhancing the mood. Likewise, the moment Constance first appeared in ‘Spindlewood’ was wonderfully captured. The rippling effects in the bridge scene were another lovely touch. ‘Fear and Whispers’ featured very dramatic lighting which heightened the growing tension so well, while ‘If You Could See My Heart (reprise)’ was visually stunning, with powerful backlighting and beams cutting through haze to create a very powerful effect. Moments like these showed exactly how effective lighting can be when fully focused on atmosphere and storytelling.

Sound was in extremely capable hands throughout. There was great warmth and balance from the orchestra. There was a lovely clarity within the orchestra mix too, with key instruments featured when required. The vocal sound was equally impressive. Mic EQ levels had been carefully set, giving a warm and full sound for both dialogue and singing. There was great balance too in the ensemble and choral work. With so many microphones in use and so many busy ensemble sequences in the show, this was all the more impressive. The sound effects work was also excellent throughout. Effects such as the turning of Constance’s key and the sound of running water were very well chosen and timed perfectly within the action.

The costume design complemented the fairytale atmosphere of the production and worked very well within the steampunk-inspired visual. The costumes hinted at a rustic, old-world setting through the use of waistcoats, aprons, layered skirts, braces and earthy fabrics. There was nice individuality within the villagers’ costumes, adding greatly to the authenticity. Constance’s costumes reflected the character’s innocence and uniqueness extremely well. Her green dress during ‘Raise a Glass’ was especially striking, setting her apart while drawing the audience’s eye towards her during what was one of the production’s biggest ensemble numbers. Excellent work from all involved.

The props department did superb work throughout, with excellent attention to detail. Abraham’s workshop in particular was beautifully realised and detailed. The various plans and sketches were beautifully realised and the clocks, books, tools and mechanical objects, ensured that the workshop looked most authentic. Mayor Glynn’s all-important pocket watch was another excellent prop choice. The market scene also featured great props work. The crates, logs and fish brought excellent life to ‘Market Day’.

Hair and makeup were very strong throughout. Constance’s look was especially impressive with an almost porcelain quality to her appearance, while the subtle mechanical influence within her eye makeup was a very clever touch. Mayor Glynn’s wig, sideburns and moustache suited his character perfectly. Male ensemble members’ sideburns were also very authentic and reinforced the overall attention to detail from the hair and makeup department.

Avonmore Musical Society’s production of ‘The Clockmaker’s Daughter’ was, above all else, a show full of heart. Underneath the fantasy, clockwork imagery and fairytale atmosphere was a beautiful story, so well told by a wonderful production team, cast and crew. There was something really uplifting about spending an evening watching a show packed with imagination and magic. Avonmore Musical Society should be very proud of what they achieved. It was a beautiful night of theatre.
reviews.wix_title: Review: The Clockmaker’s Daughter - Avonmore Musical Society

reviews.review_text:
The evenings were getting brighter and it was so lovely to arrive in daylight before the sunset following a drive through Dublin City Centre in all its glory on such a lovely sunny Spring evening. And as I arrived at St Patricks DCU this vast complex that thousands call home I was in awe of this vast building and it's gorgeous grounds in our capital city. I could have been in the countryside such is the impressiveness of the size of the buildings and the land it stands on and it's surrounds. Breath-taking. This is a hall and when I arrived, hundreds of people spilled into the Theatre's vast entrance area. The front-of-house group had a gorgeous air of calmness, laughter, and confidence.

Ms Amy McLoughlin was the Director of this production. I liked Ms. McLoughlin's direction very much. Ms McLoughlin displayed a lovely clarity and strict adherence to the spirit of the original material and film in this production. There was a gorgeous brightness and energy throughout this, and the essential themes of empowerment and self-discovery came across very well through many of the roles. I liked the directors' use of space on the stage, and the different levels and depths added layers to the critical moments in the show, with superb use of the background and foreground. The comedic timings were so well executed, and there were many, but also so many gorgeous, emotional moments that were beautiful in themselves; along with the fun, there was a lovely story underneath and lessons to be learned.

The Musical Director was Georgia Goodall. Backing Tracks were used for the accompaniment in this production, and they worked exceptionally well. It is not always easy to combine backing tracks with stage production, given timings and set changes, and to stick to the rhythm, which can be pretty constraining, with a live orchestra being more accessible to move and accompany. Whereas here, it did work well. The sound was excellent, the cast kept on time with every note. I must mention that Ms. Goodall and another person sitting in front of the cast on two chairs were brilliant, ensuring an extra blanket of security, I think, for the cast. Although this was not required as the cast were superb, It was still lovely to see.

The Choreographer was Abbie Nolan. Energetic, fun, and colourful always, the choreography here mirrored the upbeat nature of this show. Dance routines were excellent, technically awe-inspiring, and again enhanced the story – such as “What You Want” and “Bend and Snap.” I would imagine that the Director and Choreographer worked very well together here so that the dancers danced and most definitely told the story with excellent direction. The routines themselves were performed very well with a skilled and well-rehearsed cast.

I loved the Department Store Clothes rails that were expertly whizzed around the stage! I liked the set with Warner and Elle in the restaurant downstage right, which was very influential again, using the space on both sides of the stage. I did feel that with the pink set during the story, the “H” was challenging to see as it looked like pink on pink, and I couldn’t make out the lettering. However, this set still worked was functional and moved freely. I would like to have seen more attention to detail in it and a little more covering the stage as there were many times there was a lot of space on the stage when just one or two individuals were on it. I did feel some of the sets were a little plain, such as the panels in “Oh My God.”

In The Finale, the whole cast sat on chairs with their backs to the audience, as the story of each character and where they ended up was told, which was done well. I loved it. The brick wall effect as a set was also very clever and functional.

The lighting was indeed lovely. Particular mention of the beautiful colours, such as the scene “Ireland” and the Delta Nu scene. The vibrant, gorgeous colours were bright, cheerful, and fun. Lighting transitioned smoothly through each scene, and I loved the cooler tones, such as those in the courtroom, with far more formality contrasting deeply with the warm, bright lights in the Delta Nu scenes for example. The use of spotlights was glorious throughout.

The sound was very effective, and the dialogue and lyrics were delivered clearly and crisply. The clarity and precision of the dialogue and lyrics were equally outstanding, making it easy to follow along with the story, even in the most fast-paced scenes. Also, the balance between the vocals and backing tracks was spot on, and the sound levels were consistent throughout the entire performance, which is a difficult feat to achieve. The sound team's attention to detail was evident, as every sound effect and cue was timed perfectly, adding to the overall experience and making the show even more enjoyable. The sound quality was excellent, and there were no issues with feedback or distortion, making it a seamless experience for the audience.

The costumes were stunning and beautifully tailored to each character’s personality and style.. I loved Paulette's costume in Act 1. Elle’s costumes were all very chic and elegant, especially the attention to detail on the navy blue office suit for the courtroom scene, to mention but one. The dramatic change in Emmet after his visit to the Department Store with Elle was fabulous and a great scene. They used pink, which was prominent throughout the entire production, a signature colour for the show, and it was beautiful to see how it was incorporated into each costume in different ways. The costumes for the Delta Nu sorority sisters were awe-inspiring, and the costumes for the courtroom scene were also very well done with more formal attire and subtle colour tones, particularly mention to Vivienne’s Costume and, indeed, Warner’s. Superb. Overall, the costumes added to the show's vibrancy and were crucial in bringing the characters to life.

The hair and makeup for each character was well done. The attention to detail was evident with each character's unique and distinguishable look. Using bright and bold colours for the Delta Nu sorority sisters’ makeup was a great touch and added I’m sure to their energetic personalities. The hair was styled differently to suit each character, from Elle’s signature blonde locks to Paulette’s curly hair. The makeup for the courtroom scene was also very well done with a more natural look, which was appropriate for the setting.

The use of props was good, especially in the case of the two dogs. The thong belonging to Carlos brought the house down, the encyclopaedias, used for reference, were excellent, and Elle's handbag, which she never went anywhere without, were standout moments and props in the show, which were very good and highly appropriate.

The gorgeous Aisling Leahy played the part of Elle Woods. Ms. Leahy was a standout performance that genuinely captured the vivaciousness, humour, and determination of Elle Woods. Ms Leahy's vocals were excellent throughout, looked very good, and had lovely costumes. Ms Leahy had a fantastic energy and a spring in her step that was enviable, and she was just a beautiful Elle inside and out and a great friend. Lovely dialogue, gorgeous stage presence, and overall, a delightful Elle. Ms Leahy was most definitely a star of the show: superb performance, and congratulations.

Eanna Kavanagh played Emmett Forrest. Equally impressive, with his heartfelt portrayal of this lovely character, Mr Kavanagh had the audience in the palm of his hand from the moment he arrived on stage with his gorgeous, gentlemanly, shy demeanour and just his lovely star qualities as a friend and student with lovely acting ability and a beautiful stage presence.

Mr Kavanagh's stage chemistry with Elle was palpable and added great depth to the storyline. The scene in the department store was fantastic, and the transformation as you emerged as the well-dressed absolute gentleman was so well done. The transformation was jaw-dropping. Mr. Kavanagh and Ms. Leahy as Elle acted well together, and it was a joy to watch Mr. Kavanagh on stage in this role.

Jude Olurotimi-Omole played the part of Warner Huntington 11 1, and what a cool dude this gentleman was in this role. Mr Olurotimi-Omole had a significant stage presence; he looked fabulous and acted well. His words were both comical and yet very convincing. The scene where Mr. Olurotimi-Omole as Warner met Elle in the restaurant to break up with her was a highlight, especially in his calmness and authority when Elle understands it to be a proposal. You played a blinder here in this role, and I congratulate you. Well done. Superb

Olivia Foley played the part of Vivienne Kensington. This was another standout performance, with her sharp-tongued and ambitious character brought to life with a dry wit, disdain for Elle, and magnificent acting; this excellent role was brilliantly acted. Ms Foley looked great and was a tour de force on stage. She had super diction, too, and when eventually her disdain and jealousy for Elle dissipated, it was lovely to see the character change. It was moving—well done, Ms Foley.

Serena, Pilar, and Margot, played by Triona Mulvey, Annika Chow, and Emma Duff, were an utterly dynamic trio who brought great humour and energy to their roles. Their harmonies were spot-on, and their comedic timing was impeccable. These girls were simply fabulous, brilliantly cast, acted, and sang with your hearts, and in the end, these young ladies' hearts burst with pride for Elle. It was so lovely. It was an emotional moment, such as their pride for their gorgeous friend. Great costumes, fun, and beautiful. It was simply a joy to watch these three young ladies in these three roles.

Laura Rourke played Paulette. I loved Ms. Rourke in this role. This was an excellent performance by Ms. Rourke, with her sassy and gorgeous character brought to life with great flair and humour. The scenes with Paulette and Elle were standout successes. Ms. Rourke has a fabulous voice, and “Ireland” was simply gorgeous. Sung from her heart, it was great. Great costume, the lovely friendship between Ms Rourke and Elle was enviable, and what a magnificent duo Ms Rourke made with Kyle / Dewy, played by Sam Kennedy.

Caragh Davis played the part of Brooke Wyndham. Equally impressive, with her athletic and energetic performance in the "Whipped Into Shape" number being a particular highlight, I was tired even watching this young lady as she was simply fabulous in this role. Ms Davis looked the part, acted the part, and acted so well that I felt sorry for her when she had to reveal her alibi. This was a gorgeous part and a huge key in the overall story, and Ms Davis, you were super as Brooke Wyndham.

Patrick Fox played the part of Professor Callahan. What a fantastic interpretation of this role. Dressed impeccably, he looked the part, acted the part, moved around the stage confidently, and left a lasting impression on me in this role. Well done, Mr Fox.

Frances O'Neill played the part of Enid Hoopes. Ms. O’Neill’s facial expressions were hilarious. Ms Hoopes had such a lovely, fun, and serious personality. Acted intensely, revealing a tremendous character who added much to the production.

Sam Kennedy played Dewey/ Kyle. What great roles! It was so funny, very well acted, and simply excellent comedic timing—a memorable character who added a lot of personality to the show.

This gorgeous chorus was crucial in this uplifting production. The backbone of the show, great supporters of Elle Woods, brought her world to life with beautiful melodies and lovely harmonies. You were law students, Salon owners, Courtroom Attendees, and Witnesses. I can't begin to imagine how you all played different roles throughout the show, not just one – a sure testament to the talent on stage for this production. The Chorus was outstanding here, with so much vocal power and energy it was mesmerizing. As a group, you enhanced an already strong output and made a huge impact. You were one of the most vital parts of this production, and I looked forward to you coming on stage each time. I applaud you. Well done.

I thank you all and wish you all well in the future. I hope many of you involve stage and theatre in some shape or form because this group, your group, had talent in bucketloads. I wish you all well and bravo on a wonderful production and a truly lovely evening of entertainment.

reviews.review_text:
I whole-heartedly applaud the effort of Director, Brian Logan, to draw the obvious parallel between this historical story and the current plight of the Ukrainian people. This was done particularly well with the “History Repeats Itself” section of the show program, but also with a pre-prologue voice over and sound effects of an on-going war. A soldier entered from the audience, looking to the sky as planes flew overhead, and as the sounds faded, he removed his camouflage coat and ambled into his prologue as Tevye. Different and imaginative. With one of the best written books for a musical, combined with beautiful authentic music that encapsulates the time and place of the setting, Fiddler on the Roof has long been one of my favourite musicals. It’s a story of fortitude and stoicism amid the most awful adversity, but also a story of family, of love and of religious passion, with all its positive and its negative implications. The simplicity of viewing all of life through the eyes of one humble milkman is the touch of genius that makes the whole package work so brilliantly.

The show had good pace that was interrupted only by slightly laboured scene changes, sometimes with what seemed like unnecessary movement of some pieces. While the set for the show had a good rustic feel about it, there were occasions when the moving pieces seemed a little abstract. It was nicely constructed and well-painted though. There seemed to be a lot of Americanization of accents during the show, possibly following that annoying aspect of the movie version, but many characters maintained their Eastern European accents better than others. There were also occasions when comedy was lost, for example, the joke of ‘the new arrival at Motel and Tzeitel’s’ lost its impact because the sewing machine was clear to see from the start of the scene.

Musically, the show was very solid indeed, due in part to a fine orchestra, led by Musical Director, Andrew Robinson, who appreciated the feel and rhythm of the traditional Jewish style of music that permeates this score. The Fiddle playing throughout was very good indeed. Andrew also ensured that the orchestra were well-balanced with the vocals from a disciplined chorus and the strongly reliable principal singers. In Sabbath Prayer and Sunrise Sunset, in particular, the harmonies were rich and delightful. The tricky Nightmare number was also very well performed.

Choreographers Sharon Logan and Laura Fisher got the showoff to a good start with a nicely drilled display of patterns and movement for “Tradition.” There was good movement too in the “To Life” number, and their Russian soldiers made a good attempt at some difficult steps. The wedding was a lot of fun, but I’d prefer to see an attempt at an authentic bottle dance with real bottles. The “Matchmaker” number and the “Chavalet” ballet were nicely designed and executed.

The mammoth role of Tevye was played by Alan McClarty, with many moments of strong emotion and pathos, particularly in Act Two, when he struggled with losing Hodel and then Chava. These were his best scenes. I was a little distracted by his accent, which fluctuated between the expected Russian slant and some very American-sounding passages, and on one or two occasions, his dialogue was a little rushed. Particularly in his monologues to God, perhaps a slightly more pensive or undecided hesitancy might have been appropriate. I’m

delighted to say that my favourite pieces in the show, “Chavalet” and “Do You Love Me” were beautifully handled. He also gave a good robust performance of “If I Were A Rich Man.” It was a lovely touch, too, that he collected his camouflage jacket and took it with him as he left Anatevka.

Úna Culkin’s Golde was delightfully abrupt and impatient with her family members, beautifully tolerant of her encounters with Yente, and her distress at losing her daughter was very palpable. This was a very nicely played role, with good vocal quality and fine emotions. Olive Hemphill made a very convincing Yente, nicely befuddled in trying to impart her news, looking, and acting just right, and despite forgetting a line or two, she maintained her character very well throughout.

Paul Sleet was a gentle and amiable Lazar Wolf in his first encounter with Tevye but showed a good more aggrieved countenance during the wedding scene. He sang well beside Alan in the “Too Life” number.

Clare Campbell was a lovely Tzeitel, particularly in her acting when her father tried to force her to marry Lazar. There was a good genuine bond between herself and Motel, and she sang delightfully, albeit with, again, an American twang.

Patrick Connor gave a nice light comedic portrayal of Motel the Tailor, scared of his own shadow, but somehow summoning up the courage to stand up to Tevye when the chips were down. His “Miracle of Miracles” was abundant with joy, and he sustained his character beautifully throughout the show.

Megan Paul was a sincere and impetuous Hodel, quick to challenge the attitudes of Perchik, but susceptible enough to be moved by his authenticity. She played her relationship with her father very well, and “Far From The Home I Love” was nicely delivered. Adam Goudy was a spirited and forthright Perchik, full of idealism yet open to change. This was played at just the right level, making him likeable to Hodel and earning the respect of Tevye. “Now I Have Everything” was sung with sincerity.

Chloe Freeman-Wallace played young Chava with assurance and vulnerability, handling her relationship with Fyedka with caution but caring. Her passionate pleading to her father was a most touching scene.

Steven Millar was a respectful Fyedka, gentle in his approaches to Chava, and cautious in crossing her father, yet strong when he needed to be. Nicely played.

As the town busy-body, Tom Waddell was a convincing Avram, while Jim Everett had good self-importance as innkeeper, Mordcha. David McDowell was suitably pompous and uppity as Mendel, the Rabbi’s son, and Harry Stinson was a suitably dithery Rabbi. There was a condescending tone about Greg Edwards as the Constable, but his character has more depth if he shows more reluctance about the pogrom that disrupts the wedding. Richard Campbell looked well and played extremely well as The Fiddler. There were very good cameo performances by Vicky Hogg as Grandma Tzeitel, and Kellyann McKillen sang splendidly in a fine and original representation of Fruma Sara. Lesley Reynolds as Shandel, Adam Campbell as Nachum and Steve Setterfield as Sasha all contributed well to the overall performance.

Sphrintze and Bielke were delightfully played by Ela Richards and Sophie O’Neill, with nice character and good clear voices.

Perhaps the Chorus could have been a little more challenged in their dancing, but they performed all that was asked of them with good confidence. Their reactions to the drama around them was good and vocally, they were very secure. “Sabbath Prayer,” “Sunrise Sunset” and “Anatevka” were all very easy on the ear.

There was good attention to detail in the costuming of the show, prayer shawls in place and heads covered as one would expect. Russian outfits were good too, and the principal characters all seemed to be appropriately attired to suit their individuality. There was good work done on beards, etc., and make-up was perfectly fine, with nice attention to Grandma Tzeitel and a good novel approach to the presentation of Fruma Sara. Props and stage dressing were good throughout. Likewise, the lighting was generally quite good, providing atmosphere for many scenes and more often than not effectively highlighting the main action.

The crew, under stage manager, David Wray, sometimes seemed uncertain of where each piece was to be positioned, but they went about their task with decent efficiency. The sound for the show was very satisfactory.

My thanks to all involved in the many Ballywillan shows that I have enjoyed over the years, and I wish you good fortune and many wonderful productions in the future.
reviews.wix_title: Fiddler on the Roof as presented by Ballywillan Drama Group

reviews.review_text:
Guys and Dolls was inspired by the writings of Damon Runyon, who based his writings on his experiences and characters encountered in and around the Broadway area of the 1930’s. Inspired by the Runyon - Frank Loesser, Jo Swirling and Abe Burrows conspired to crunch together a number of short stories into what we now know as Guys’n’Dolls the Musical.

Belfast Operatic chose this musical, it appears from the programme, for the first time, and produced a fine interpretation. Belfast Operatic are blessed with the amazing Grand Opera House in which to present their shows and this alone should be an inspiration to any production. The Opera house was renovated recently in June 2021. They added a beautiful atrium to the side of the theatre which now acts as the entrance foyer and have lovingly restored the interior to a very high standard.

The first thing I noticed, after staring in wonder at the beautifully ornate décor in the theatre, was a very large orchestra pit with a very large orchestra. Aside from this being my first outing as adjudicator in the new Opera House another first for me was the presence of a sign language interpreter throughout the production.

In the Director’s chair for this production, was Kerry Rodgers. Ms. Rodgers had a very clear vision for the look of this show, it began with a gauze onto which there were gobos with various motifs of dice and cards etc., and a lone desk in front. As the overture commenced this was filled with a person seemingly typing at the desk and as the chorus entered and moved around with various newspapers with large text, it was evident this was to represent the above-mentioned Damon Runyon, who’s stories inspired the original production. Along with this behind the gauze appeared various montages with cast members giving little hints and tasters of what was to come.

Her use of dice as the main focal point of the production, as chairs, tables, stairways, and even phone holders worked really well, and I liked the consistency of the theme. Where it didn’t resonate quite so well, was in the Havana scene and in the sewer scene where along with the very distinctive markings on the floor the look was very much the same.

I didn’t like the staging of Adelaide’s “Lament”. I was confused as to whether it was supposed to be her dressing room, or the hot box, and this scene as mentioned elsewhere would have benefitted from clearer, more defined lighting restricting it to a certain area. Using the whole stage – again with the very large markings took away from any sense of place.

Ms. Rodgers work with the chorus was evident as the show took flight with very effective groupings and images throughout the production. I’m guessing there was close collaboration with the choreographer for the Havana scene, particularly in the tour of historic places in Havana. The use of the chorus here representing statues, buildings, archways etc. was very effective.

Colin Scott had charge of the above-mentioned 19-piece orchestra, and from the opening note to the last toot of the finale he was in total control. His work with a very talented group of singers was evident throughout the production, all principals sang very well, and they were supported by an orchestra which in theory should have drowned out much of the singing, but in Mr. Scotts hands they had no concerns, and along with a very efficient sound design we could hear every note of every song. Harmonies were also very clear and bravo to a very well-rehearsed chorus for their support and delivery in all the chorus numbers. A choral highlight of this production, and I suppose most productions of Guys’n’Dolls, was of course “Sit Down You’re Rockin’ the Boat”. We could hear all 4 parts distinctly throughout. However, respect is also due to the “guys” who produced a very energetic and well sung version of “Luck be a Lady”.

Timothy Bell returns again as Choreographer for this production, and he worked well with the director to deliver a very energetic and effective set of routines. Guys’n’Dolls can often get carved up into the Hot Box scenes for the dancing girls and the “Luck be a Lady” and “Sit Down” for the guys, but Mr. Bell ensured that there was as much to do for the full chorus as possible. This was evident from the start in the various scenes depicting Broadway, and in almost every number outside of the big numbers to depict the various images painted by the lyrics. Perhaps most impressive was the use of the chorus in Havana as the various sight-seeing points that Sarah was determined to see, and they added greatly to the effect. There was a very full stage for the dance number in Havana, and this was danced and moved very nicely. The crap shooters ball and Luck be a Lady were very well-staged and executed with the full company of men providing a riot of colour and energy, whilst singing very well - and this was most impressive. There was also very impressive “Hatograpghy” on display from the guys in “Good Old Reliable”, the first big chorus number and this kicked off the production nicely.

Sky Masterson was played by Dessie Havlin, and he gave a nice interpretation of the role. As with all the principals he had a singing voice that was well trained, strong and suited to the range of the various songs. “My Time of Day” was well sung, leading into the beautiful duet “I’ve Never Been in Love Before”.

Sarah Brown – Naomi Smyth – had a beautiful soprano voice and she excelled in all her songs. “I’ve Never Been in Love Before” was beautiful from both. Pretending to choke whilst drinking in “Marry the Man” was excellent. I felt there could have been more made of the drinking scene in Havana, there needed to be a few more coconuts for her to drink from. Ms. Smyth was every bit the prim and proper Sarah Brown.

Greg Fox - Nathan Detroit – yet another beautiful singing voice, a feature of this very musically talented cast. I thought his accent was a bit patchy in his opening few lines, but he warmed up quickly and maintained a good level for the remainder of the performance. Nathan took full part in the crapshooters dance as well as “Luck be a Lady” and danced very well.

Adelaide – Emiko Seawright – was a wonderful singer and had a good consistent accent throughout. I must confess I didn’t like her wig – it was poorly styled as were many of the other Hot Box girls. As mentioned above her “Lament” suffered from too much movement around the stage, but the “Lament” reprise worked better, as she remained in one place and this gave her the opportunity to tell the story.

Nicely – Conor Anderson – sang well from the beginning. His intro into “guys and dolls” song from the preceding dialogue was a bit rushed timing wise. I felt that whilst they both sang well, both Benny and Nicely were lost and at times upstaged with the various couples/activities happening around them.

Benny – Daniel Clarke. Good supporting performance from this actor and a strong contribution to both the three-hander in “Fugue” and the two-hander in the “Guys’n’Dolls” numbers. I felt that both he and Nicely could have been dressed a bit “louder” to make them stand out from the other gangsters.

Rusty – Adam Callander. The third wheel in the opening “fugue” was a strong singer and supported the other two with ease.

Brannigan – Kevin McIlhennon, had a nice consistent accent, and good costume. His early scenes with Nathan and the gamblers were well handled but I felt the entrance in the mission scene for “Sit Down” could have been handled better.

General Cartwright - Laura Kerr – was calm, poised and gave a strong and well-judged performance as the General. A cameo yes, but Ms. Kerr demonstrated confidence in her character and delivered her lines with conviction.

Arvide – Michael Bradley. “More I Cannot Wish You” is always a difficult scene and song but Mr. Bradley handled it well and sung in a gentle and appropriate manner.

Big Jule – Luke Allen – was introduced by Harry and started very twitchy but didn’t maintain this, so it was confusing to the audience what he was trying to portray. He waved (and revealed) his gun too early, and this was clearly seen by Brannigan. Timing of dialogue was rushed in places, and for me was - too jokey throughout.

Harry – James Marsden. A good supporting role from this young man, although some lines were either lost or dropped, e.g. the “buick” line was completely inaudible, and the “show me where it says that in Hoyle” completely lost.

Agatha – Emma McCourt, played with the right amount of gravitas in the mission scenes where she featured.

Joey – Rachel Halliday –adopted a good persona for this character, but I didn’t like the gun piece – it didn’t seem appropriate (looked like a red water pistol). I liked the dice as holders for the phones.

Mimi – Kathryn Aiken, timed her “looking for an earring” scene well and delivered her lines with great confidence. I loved that she found the earring in her hair!

Mistress of ceremonies – India Clements and Claire Howell, Angie - Lucas Levy and Society Max – Oliver Stevenson, were good in their supporting roles as were all the gangsters/gamblers.

The Chorus in Belfast Operatic were on show from the beginning behind the gauze with well staged montages of various scenes. Along with the principal players they sang very well, and all harmonies were clear and correct. The chorus particularly impressed in the Havana scenes, initially as the human versions of landmarks and places that Sarah wished to see, and afterwards as a full ensemble dancing in the Havana/pre-fight scene. Guys were excellent in the all-male numbers and in particular the “Crapshooters Ballet” and “Luck be a Lady” were highlights. The Ladies in the Hot Box numbers sang and danced well and both numbers were well received.

The Stage Manager was the very experienced – Andy McKnight. As mentioned above the majority of props were various sizes of dice used as tables chairs and trees, lamps etc., along with one staircase – again dressed as dice, and these were all moved on and off by the cast. There were appropriately styled chairs for the mission scenes and again these were moved by cast. There was one moment of delay between removing boxes/dice and bringing on mission furniture, but this was minor. The stairs – which was the largest piece, was moved effortlessly by cast and principals throughout the performance and as I found out afterwards there was ample room both sides of the stage to store these. The stairs disappeared for Havana, although the same dice were used as furniture, and I felt it needed something different to distinguish it from New York. Same for the sewer scene, and the “If I Were a Bell” scene - no distinction. They needed something different, particularly given the very strong and distinctive markings on the floor.

Lighting – good in “Good Old Reliable”, effective at start with gobos and images behind gauze, nice spotlight for the “jack of spades” line in the scene with Nathan and Sky. Nice feel to the lights at the end of “I’ll Know” but felt they were a bit too bright at start of the “Lament” scene, also too bright at the start of “My Time of Day”. I felt that for some of the interior scenes the use of very discreet lighting of just certain parts of the stage e.g. in “Lament” and “Interior Mission” would have added to the look.

Sound – excellent throughout with balance of orchestra and mics perfect. With such a large room, band and cast we could hear all the individual principals over the orchestra, and the harmonies were also mixed well. Good collaboration between the MD and the Sound Designer.

Makeup and wigs – I noted that there was no mention of a makeup or wig person so assume cast looked after their own. This was evident in some of the styling of the wigs and for me some were not tidy enough and of the period. Costumes – overall good, the “take back your mink” dresses looked like they had seen better days, and although I liked the “bushel” dresses, a second “reveal” to me took away from the big reveal in the “mink” scene. I wondered about men in shorts in Havana? I would also have liked a different look for the locals, maybe capri pants for some of the ladies or bolder colours. This along with the same décor, dice for tables etc. didn’t offer a different look for “Havana”. I liked the Sally Army uniforms; they fit well and were consistent. The different range of colours on display for “Luck be a Lady” scene was impressive.

Overall, this was a very enjoyable start to this new year, and a very enjoyable visit to this beautiful venue.

A society with this level of history and resources don’t need any advice from me, but for what it’s worth – and I know it’s show dependent – if there are wigs in use, they need to be of a certain standard and styled accordingly. Whilst the movement of the company in the larger chorus scenes was excellent, I felt that greater time needed to be given over to not just learning the lines, but in getting to grips with the timing of the many gags in this very funny show. There were many things to enjoy about this production, and a few tweaks here and there will almost certainly bring it to another level.

reviews.review_text:
What The Wedding Singer lacks in depth and drama, it more than makes up for with a great sense of fun and some rockin’ good music, and it’s a great tonic for an audience, who can sit back, relax and enjoy the frolics without having to engage the brain too much. Having spoken to Director, Jessica Bray, after the show, I loved her attitude to the piece, appreciating that it was a great comedic romp, entertainment for entertainment’s sake, that gave plenty of involvement for performers young and old, and that sense of fun pervaded her handling of the material. Characters were nicely exaggerated and diverse, and the romantic story was almost told tongue-in-cheek. The pace of the show was very good and technically and visually, it ticked all the right boxes.

The show employed a simple and effective, but cleverly designed set, consisting of three sets of silver slash curtains, through which props and furniture were easily moved into place, with stage right opening up to become the Dumpster area, and Julia’s bedroom, while stage left opened into Robbie’s basement bedroom in his Grandma’s house. Good stage management by Lorcan McAuliffe, saw changes occur tidily with little interruption to the flow of the show. Props were generally very good and appropriate, and while the Car front used by Glen in his opening scene was clever, it was a tad dilapidated for such a wealthy guy. The show was nicely costumed, with all the necessary trappings of the wedding functions, good brides’ dresses, nice outfits for the band, and the waitresses distinctive from the guests. The wide range of hairstyles, as with the costumes, were always appropriate to the era of the show and there were no problems with make-up.

Musical Director, Shane Farrell, led a very fine band with good authority and very good tempi and tone throughout the show. Everything was well-paced, and there was a good balance between the pounding rhythms of the dance numbers and the more mellow tones of the romantic songs. There was good balance too between pit and stage, allowing the good harmonies and fine diction of the chorus, under Chorus Mistress, Eilis O’Neill, to be clearly heard. With accomplished principal vocalists as well, this was a safe and sound musical offering.

In the role of Robbie Hart, Patrick Woulfe had the charm and charisma required to be a convincing front man for the band, and there was good sincerity in his acting as well as good comedy delivery. He was vocally secure and able to accompany himself on guitar, even if the guitar did need a bit more amplification.

Cliodhna McNelis captured the warm and good-natured personality of Julia perfectly, and combined with a beautifully mellow vocal tone, it was easy to feel all of her emotions throughout the show. A very endearing performance.

Feargal Kearney, as Glen Gulia, had swagger and arrogance that fitted his loathsome character. He delivered All About The Green with great confidence, but for the most part, he was just delightfully obnoxious, which is, of course, a compliment.

Julita Fox, as Holly, lit up the stage, full of attitude and the kind of blatant sexuality that scares most men out of making a move for fear of getting a punch or maybe a disease. She hilariously embraced her inner slut while still showing signs of insecurity. Vocally, she nailed her songs with supreme confidence.

Eoin Gilmartin, as Sammy, gave a very cocky and confident performance, perfectly combining wannabe rock-star attitude and total nerdiness, that kind of friend that you put up with because you know he has a kind heart under all the bravado. Nicely played and well sung.

Sean McInerney was a delightfully camp George, without going over the top. His comedy was well-timed, and he built a good relationship with Grandma. He was also very funny in his delivery of his singing.

Hilary Orpen-Ryan aged beautifully to give zest and zany humour to the role of Grandma, really enjoying the outrageous inappropriateness of so many of her lines. This was very nicely played, with fun and energy and great vocal delivery.

Saoirse Daly made the most of slutty Rock-chick, Linda, tastefully vulgar in her gyrations, selfish and insincere in her attitude, just as the character should be. Her vocals were confidently and securely delivered.

Sarah Kenny was a suitably shallow but streetwise mother to Julia, in the role of Angie, playing with controlled ease and the relaxed stage presence that comes with good experience. A very good character comedy performance.

As well as performing strongly as a unit, many of the chorus also filled the plethora of cameo roles as brides, grooms, best men, guests, vicars, et al, and did so with talent and conviction. They were also well-rehearsed and accurate in their vocal contribution to the show As a group, they were energetic and very capable for the dancing demands. Laura-Jane Allis injected her choreography with plenty of energy and creativity, devising routines that were within the capabilities of her dancers, hence the good level of precision and delivery. I loved the twee routine for ‘Single’ and the high energy of ‘Saturday Night in the City,’ but there was good expressive work too in ‘Casualty of Love’, ‘All About The Green’ and ‘Move That Thang’. A very pleasing contribution to the show.

Many of the scenes were enhanced by good lighting, with plenty of effects for the party scenes and good colour, atmosphere and focus in the more intimate scenes. Faces and actions were well highlighted. Sound quality was fine and well-balanced, allowing voices to be clearly heard over the musicians.

Ennis Musical Society continue to impress, not just with talent, but with a warm and embracing sense of community and inclusiveness. It is evident in their front of house activities and in their hospitality, and as far as performance is concerned, one always feels that warmth emanating from the stage, and on this occasion, it led to a very pleasing and entertaining overall production. Sincere thanks to all concerned for a highly enjoyable night.

Peter Kennedy

Gilbert Adjudicator 2023/24

Photos by

John O'Neill
