Not for the first time this season, the importance of visibility was shown on an Irish musical theatre stage and themes of tolerance and love shone through. It was a wonderfully entertaining production with an important message and Kilcock MDS delivered said message with a beautiful mix of sincerity and sequins.
reviews.wix_title: Priscilla Queen of the Desert as presented by KMDS

reviews.review_text:
“True happiness comes from being who we want to be, no matter what the norm and its expectations are, and being authentically honest in who you are, no matter what the expectation of others, is enough”.

Aghada is the most picturesque and tranquil of places in the lovely East Cork, a few miles from Midleton, which I was lucky to visit on my AIMS journey this year. A new Society to AIMS, it was a joy to meet the lovely cast, crew, and locals of this beautiful place, which has been their 10th Production since being founded. “The Addams Family”. I am so happy to have the honour of being your first Adjudicator. Aghada Centre Theatre group is an exceptional group of people who, every year for the past ten years, donate ALL of their surplus funds after expenses to charity. Truly Special. Upon my arrival, I was greeted by Le-Anne Tynan, Ann-Marie O’Keeffe, Chairpersons of the Theatre Group and Helen Walsh and Front of House team. I watched the dry ice beginning to billow out from the Theatre into my path, with the cobwebs and eeriness enveloping me once I stepped into the Foyer. This foyer was decorated beautifully, so one could be forgiven for believing you were on the stage rather than the entrance. The attention to detail was so intricate, complex, and vast, with beautiful lighting and a cavernous atmosphere, which I was immediately taken by. I was given the most lovely goodie bag with both chocolate and crisps promoting local producers in the area, a precious gift bag with a big gold bow, and, of course, my program. A buzz of pride and excitement, laughter and chatter, of the patrons immediately surrounded me. Indeed, the Community of Aghada's massive support for this group was evident as I waited for the show to begin. A beautiful welcome.

Director and producer Sinead Dunlea has been involved with ACTG for ten years. This is a small stage, with every available space like gold dust and a big cast. Ms Dunlea worked this venue very well. Ms. Dunlea brought to life the dark humour and quirkiness of the Addams family with some perfect comedy moments throughout, which can indeed be difficult to marry the two effectively sometimes. However, this production had a lovely balance and worked well, bringing the show and the Addams Family story together seamlessly and effectively. Ms Dunlea’s attention to detail is everywhere in this production, from the eerie sound effects to the interactions between the various characters with their needs, struggles, and desires.

The cast were very well suited to each other visually and vocally. I loved the cascading dry ice flowing off the stage for the Overture. The entrance of the Addams family and the introductions to each character, the family dinner was superb, with the cast members coming up out of the audience to be seated along a huge intricately designed dinner table the width of the stage, and it was seamlessly moved. Everyone in place very quickly yet without rush. I loved how the cast under Ms Dunlea's direction moved slowly, smoothly, creepily, and eerily throughout. There was never a rushing or quick movement, and a relaxing ambiance was created throughout the production. It did occur to me that your direction, along with the rest of your Production team, really did have a real family feel here- pardon the pun- on and off the stage, and it was a joy to watch. There was a lovely atmosphere all around me, but in particular, what stood out for me in your role as Director were the intricacies of building your show with a small space and lots of people, along with telling the story of The Addams family. The direction here was a treat and a success for all of the above reasons, and I do say very well done to a gorgeous show and it certainly worked.

The choreographer was Aileen McMurtry. Choreography lifted this show with energy in the darkness and gloom. “Full Disclosure” was super, a significant number, slick, professional, and dramatic. “When You’re an Addams.” Gomez's moves in this were excellent, and his connection with Morticia highlighted the superb chemistry between these two actors; he moved excellently, as did Wednesday with her sharper, more rebellious movements, yet lovely all the same. The choreography showed the characters and the differences between everyone in great detail in their dance movements. The choreography added an extra layer to the ghoulish, spooky atmosphere that had already emanated from the beginning of the Overture. “When You’re an Addams,” the opening number with the Addams family introducing themselves, was an explosion of light drama, dance, and sound. “Not Today” with Gomez and Ensemble was simple and gorgeous, with the movements all around making this number a picture, a vision, and a scene of beauty. Choreography by Ms McMurtry was inventive, engaging, and seamlessly integrated into the storytelling. Attention to detail and the varying dance styles, from tango, as mentioned above, to more modern, was a visual treat for the audience and enhanced the whole production beautifully. Well, done, Ms McMurtry. Your talent in this show shone through your cast. Beautiful job.

The Musical Director was Mr Robbie Pender. Upon my arrival, I didn’t see the Orchestra in the pit; however, I did not expect to find them high up backstage on a platform built over the stage similar to the mezzanine level, looking down on the cast and the proceedings. This was a work of art and such a clever idea, and it worked beautifully, enhancing the show. The Orchestra was on stage the whole time, only up high and shielded from the cast with the various objects described above so as not to distract from the on-stage performances of the Cast “Full Disclosure” was a superb number in its chaos and comedy. “Death is just Around the Corner” with Uncle Fester, with his lovely cheerful disposition and sweet vocal, immediately caught my attention, and “Crazier than You” with Wednesday and Lucas these all were highly memorable moments in the show with beautiful emphatic accompaniment and sound with colossal respect and rapport with and for the performers beneath their feet every single second of the show. Principal cast and chorus were well rehearsed and showed confidence in their Musical director . It was obvious that great attention to detail was also done on a one to one basis as well as the ensemble. Well done.

The Stage Manager was Aoife Ryan. Design and Construction Managers were Tony O’Shea and Leonard Ryan, with the Set Construction Team, Tony O’Shea, Mili Rilov, Justin Dunlea, Declan Devoy Martin Ryan, Jason Ryan, Declan Ryan, Dave O’Shea, Bill Steele, Austin Broderick and Midleton Men’s Shed. This is a vast group and team effort, and the Set was a considerable success in-depth, solidity, and appropriateness. Given the tight space around the stage hall and backstage, the Set Design worked very well with clever use of the stage, such as placing the Orchestra above the stage, with a very secure balcony/plinth purpose-built. The sets moved smoothly, and a good team worked very well together. The sets had a very successful gothic architecture, and despite the darkness, they were glamorous. The sets were authentic. The rack-like ladder down stage right where Pugsley resided for a few moments in Act 1, was very detailed, again giving more depth to the stage, and this visually was very effective, thorough, and clever in its design and practicality. The panelled effect walls the width of the back of the stage painted in brown with the drab but gothic grey door in between them used as an entrance was very clever and, again, great attention to detail here. So well done to you, Ms Ryan, and the Design and Construction Management team. A great success indeed in this area.

The lighting and Design Engineer was David James (D2K Ltd). This lighting from the moment the curtains opened was excellent. Magnificent use of spots and colour, and no one was ever in the shadows. From the lighting of The Addams Family home to the yellows and reds in Act 1 of Morticia’s scene, they were so lovely and practical. They were lifting the darkness superbly. The scene with Gomez and Mal Beineke was lit beautifully again, with excellent use of spots, bringing the spots down through the middle aisle into the audience. I loved using the dim lighting to exaggerate the dull, gloomy, eerie atmosphere in complete contrast to the brighter lighting described above in other areas and scenes. The use of beautiful colour in the many scenes, with particular mention again for the clever use of spots, was very well done—beautiful lighting design throughout, Mr James.

Sound Engineer (D2K Ltd) Florent Sabarros, Back Stage Engineer (D2K Ltd) Luciano Costa, with Mic Caller Paul Ryan. The sound was generally excellent overall; however, there were moments during the show, particularly in Wednesday's and Morticia's dialogue, that I could not hear properly, which was slightly distracting. This mainly was in Act 1. I would have liked the mics / Radio mics to have been louder for these two characters – singing-wise, both vocals were powerful. However, it was the dialogue that I missed quite a bit of, particularly mentioning the scene with Wednesday and Lucas. And Gomez and Morticia. I still understood the story and could follow. I would have liked the speaking voices to be louder because of the balance in several numbers. Also, when the above were singing, their voices were a little lost by the sound of the Orchestra. This was no fault of the Orchestra whatsoever. I found it difficult to hear the dialogue, which is a pity as the show was glorious from beginning to end. Radio Mics could have been louder here also; however, it was only a small number of incidences that I struggled to hear.

Make-up artists and Assistants were a hell of a team. What an array of responsibility on your shoulders here to create the visions for this show, The Addams Family. The makeup was brilliant and a huge success! Gomez, Morticia, Pugsley, Grandmother, Wednesday, Uncle Festers specifically, of course, and the Chorus's makeup was sensational. I think of how many hours it took to get this right every evening in such superb detail. Bravo.

Costumes and Props & Wigs. The Costume Designer was Mary Collier and her team of Angela Barry, Magdolna Kiss, Roisin O’Sullivan, Mary Collier, Liz Callery, and Fiona Devoy. Mary and her team made beautiful costumes together from materials kindly donated by James Cooney and adapted costumes obtained from various other sources. The costumes were on point, appropriate, very professional, and authentic. I loved Gomez's dapper pinstripe suit and Morticia gown. The costumes overall were excellent, Ms Collier and team. The props were also all super throughout. Well done to the team involved in the above regions; whether your role was big or small, it does not matter. It was a huge success. Well done to every one of you.

Brian O’Riordan played Gomez. What a charming character Mr O’Riordan made of this character. Tall, brooding, dark, funny, eloquent, dramatic, and adorable all in one with a lovely singing voice and acting skills superbly cast in this vital role, he took it and made it his own, and it was a success. He is a lovely character and has a sweet connection with Morticia and his family in Wednesday, Pugsley, and Grandma Addams. An anchor character in the overall story, his love for his family and other eccentricities endeared me to him immediately—his lovely singing tone and marvellous stage presence. Well, done, Mr. O’Riordan, you were a fantastic and likable Gomez. Congratulations.

Julie Buckley played the part of Morticia Addams, Gomez's wife and mother to Pugsley and Wednesday. Visually, you were so very striking, Ms Buckley, with costume, hair makeup, props, vocals, and oh-so-wonderful dramatic facial expressions with eyes like pools of water with lovely vocals and expressions. You were a very striking Morticia, Ms Buckley, and a very successful one. You made it your own. Your relationships with your children Wednesday and Pugsley were adorable, and your face when you gave the look of disdain to anything you did not like was class! All it took was one withering look from yourself, and everyone crumbled to your wishes, demands, and rules: superb facial expression here, Ms Buckley. You were a lovely leading lady to Gomez, an excellent vocalist, and a fantastic visual. Bravo.

Willow Buckley played the part of Wednesday Addams. This young lady possesses a lovely stage presence and glorious voice and is so suited to this enjoyable role. I loved your voice. It has a clear, beautiful tone, lovely diction, and musicality, and you are very at ease in your singing and acting, Ms Buckley. Strong-willed and with your Father wrapped around your little finger, you were a firm Wednesday Addams. I did mention already under sound that I did find it hard to hear some of your lines in Act 1. Your voice could have been a little louder as I missed some of your lines – however, without hesitation, I can say your voice is gorgeous. You were a powerful link in the overall success of this show, Ms Buckley, in so many ways, as mentioned above, and I hope you continue to be a part of stage life in the future. You were indeed especially vocally a beautiful Wednesday Addams, and congratulations. I thoroughly enjoyed your performance.

Layla Rose O’Shea played Pugsley Addams and what a lovely character, Ms O’Shea. From the moment you arrived on stage, I was taken by your expression, especially your eyes, your costume and your makeup. Along with this, you were so relaxed in every part of this show; you suited this part very well and were very well directed, and I believe that you enjoyed this role immensely from what I saw. At 12 years of age, and this being your very first Musical production, you are a natural on stage. Mischievous and lovable, you were a lovely Pugsley Addams, and I hope you continue your journey on stage now after your first Musical here with this lovely group. Well, you're done, Ms O’Shea. It is a joy to watch you in this role as Pugsley Addams.

Patrick Kirwan played the part of Uncle Fester Addams. Beautiful role. You have a lovely character, great costume, and beautiful vocals, Mr Kirwan. You were a delight each time you came on stage to sing or to act. Your song To the Moon was a highlight of the show for me. It was so softly sung with such feeling with the ensemble around you, and your song of love was simply so moving, bright, and full of love. With your contrast to the darkness of the Addams family story, you created a balance that knitted the emotions of this show together to create its success. This was a fantastic role for you, Mr Kirwan. Well, you were done.

Orla Burke played the part of Grandma Addams. Magnificent role, Ms Burke. Your hair, costume, walk, stoop, teeth, and voice all added to a Grandma Addams, who was beautiful on stage and an exceptional character in this lovely show. You moved so quickly around the stage that it's obvious you are no stranger to it, and your costume was so well made it stood out. Quirky, scary (the makeup!), vocal, able to stand up for yourself without fear, and a charming stage presence. This was such an enjoyable cameo role in this show that you performed an exceptionally high acting talent and stagecraft. You were awesome, Ms Burke, in every way in this role. Congratulations.

Milivoj Rilov played the part of Lurch. What a scary Lurch you made from the word go. That hand on your shoulder was marvellous but very scary at the same time. Your height alone gave you an excellent visual stage presence, and you were very influential in your role. It was your voice. Your unique bass voice blew me away when you sang. There was a strength, force, and quality behind your voice here that is rare. It was wonderful. What a fabulous part you played here, Mr Rilov. Magnificent in this role. Bravo.

Elvira Walsh played the part of Alice. Firstly, you had a lovely stage appearance, softly spoken and mannerly. I loved your yellow dress like a beacon in the darkness, and this part suited you. With stunning acting and gorgeous singing voices, you and Mal, your husband, played by Wayne McSweeney, were a lovely couple on stage with excellent rapport and stage chemistry between you both. Nothing seemed to disturb or perplex you about the Addams family, and you also had a lovely singing voice. I liked your role in this, Ms Walsh. There is a complete contrast in nearly every aspect of your character compared to the Addams family. It didn’t take a whisker out of you. It was a significant part, a lovely role, acted and sung beautifully, Ms Walsh, and well done.

Wayne McSweeney played the part of Mal Beineke. This was a lovely role, imposing business-like character and Lucas's Dad and husband to Alice. Trying to do the best for your son, meet the future in-laws, behave accordingly, and try not to be shocked by many of the intricate running’s of the Addams family themselves. Lovely movement on stage, confident and assured, and impeccably dressed. Lovely voice. Well, you done, McSweeney. You were a wonderful Mal Beineke. Congratulations on a charming performance all around.

Jack O’Leary played the part of Lucas. In love with Wednesday Addams, the contrast created between yourself and Wednesday initially was very well done. You dressed as a city gentleman and Wednesday in her dark gothic-like character, but you did look good together, and you both had a lovely rapport. Perfectly cast, it was a joy to watch you on stage, and I enjoyed what you made of this lovely role. I wish you well and hope you continue participating in Theatre / Musical life in the future.

I was genuinely amazed at this group's care, honour, and generosity, raising much-needed funds for various Charities for the last ten years and this year is no different. Thank you for allowing me to witness your show, and I wish you many years of continued success from the bottom of my heart. You are a unique bunch, and I will never forget you. Bravo. It was indeed a pleasure.
reviews.wix_title: The Addams Family as presented by Aghada Centre Theatre Group

reviews.review_text:
There’s very little subtlety about the currently very popular new Musical version of Mel Brook’s Young Frankenstein, and it requires a company that isn’t afraid to go for the comedy jugular to show it to its full potential. Thankfully, St. Agnes had a cast who didn’t hold back on the silliness and totally immersed themselves in their characters.

Indeed, Director, Rachel Logan-Fee, did a great job of casting this show, and of making sure that each character had strong and appropriate individuality. She presented good pictures on the stage and used the space well. The chorus were integrated nicely into the action and always with a good sense of purpose. While there was a strong emphasis on the comedy of the show, a few lines were thrown away or not as strongly delivered, and perhaps some of the risqué humour could have been even more exaggerated. Technically, a screen, centre stage, was efficient for projecting location, etc., for the benefit of the audience, and perhaps could have been used more for special effects. The solid set around it was nicely designed and well-painted, but was a little cumbersome, giving Stage Manager, Andy McKnight and his team, quite a task with the scene changes. They managed well, though, working as speedily as they could.

While most scenes were nicely presented, Frankenstein’s laboratory was disappointing. With the creation of the Monster being the dramatic high point of the show, much more effort is needed to go into making it a spectacular happening. Perhaps a rising platform, with billowing smoke, much more flashing lights, much more electrical equipment, like jump leads attached to the monster, frightening thunder and lightning effects, a dark foreboding atmosphere. Unfortunately, what we got was rather lame and didn’t have that massive impact. Sparks did fly, but they were limited, and the scene was too brightly lit for them to dazzle us. Similarly, the brain-swap between Frankenstein and the Monster needed a bit more creativity and spectacle. Lighting throughout the rest of the show was good and very satisfactory, using nice colour sequences and moving lights. There was also good mood lighting for the more intimate scenes.

Musical Director, Andrew Robinson, kept very good control of a most capable and accomplished orchestra, with well-dictated rhythms, good mellow tones, when required, and very good balance throughout. With the chorus sounding musically strong and robust in their harmonies, it was evident that good rehearsal had gone into their preparation. The show was musically and vocally most impressive.

The show opened strongly, with a good energetic rendition of ‘The Happiest Town’, and indeed, Choreographer, Amy Blackshaw, in all of her routines, had a chorus and dancers who made the most of their opportunities to shine. Amy’s best work came in the shape of “Puttin’ on the Ritz”, which was the terpsichorean treat of the show, being stylish, creative and very nicely performed. The chorus were energetic and pretty disciplined in all their dancing and moving, and they contributed good acting and reacting throughout the show.

Taking the lead as Dr. Frederick Frankenstein, Allen Gordon, looking like a cross between Albert Einstein and Groucho Marx, gave a strong and highly amusing performance, comically struggling to disassociate himself from his family name, but being easily lured back to his roots. His singing and his delivery of lines was articulate and impressive, and he played all his comedic encounters with good timing and expression. I loved his tolerance of his fiancé and his easily manipulated desire for Inga.

Thomas Martin was a strong physical comedian in the role of Igor, his look and his mannerisms fitting so well with the character. His line delivery was also very good, and he developed his relationship with the Doctor very well. Added to that, was a fine voice and more importantly, an ability to sell his lyrics.

Michelle Hannaway played the self-absorbed, narcissist, Elizabeth Benning to a T. Her demeanour, her voice and her attitude were all perfectly in keeping with the vanity of her character, and she used them all to great comedic effect. She also knows how to deliver a song, with great expression and quality vocals. ‘Deep Love’ wasn’t just funny, it was filthy, and I… I mean we, as an audience, loved it.

Sassy and sexy in a much more earthy and unpretentious manner was Lorraine Jackson’s Inga, a titivating tease, ready to fulfil all the doctor’s needs, at work and at play. Lorraine had a great accent, great dance ability, great delivery of her songs, especially her yodelling, and showed no discomfort at all at being the promiscuous, scantily clad eye-candy of the piece.

And then there was Frau Blúcher, the housekeeper from hell, with evil eyes, a flippant and fearless attitude, and superb comic delivery, as played by Emma Nugent. This was the performance of the show for me, even though I think she had the potential to be even funnier. Some visual gags were missing, and I do think she could have been made-up to be even more comically sinister. Still, she almost stole the show with ‘He Was My Boyfriend’, and her every line brought rapturous laughter from the audience.

Martin McDowell, had he been given an extra foot of height, would have been perfect as The Monster, for in every other respect, he was excellent. He had a great ability to change his facial expression from sad and pathetic to angry and terrifying, and his grunting and whimpering were delightfully animalistic. His comedic timing was spot on, and he looked superb, thanks to a great costume and fabulous make-up.

Ditanya McKinty gave a strong character performance as Inspector Kemp, playing her with an almost military, disciplinarian attitude. Secure in her music and her dialogue, perhaps her potential to be more comedic was reduced by omitting the physical gags of prosthetic limbs.

One always assumes, in the movie, that the Inspector probably lost his arm in an encounter with the original monster, hence his strong desire to get rid of the Frankensteins. Nevertheless, this was a well-played role.

The only drawback to having a female Hermit, very nicely portrayed by Gemma Duffy, is that it requires Frau Blúcher to switch her sexual preferences from a man (Dr. Victor Von Frankenstein) to a woman, when she excuses herself to go on ‘a blind date’. Regardless of that, Gemma Duffy played her well and delivered her song with good comedy.

Andrew Johnston made a worthy contribution as Dr. Victor, stepping out of his very effective portrait frame, and Chris Mooney was a guileless and quirky Ziggy, the village idiot who was actually quite smart.

From a visual perspective, the show was very nice indeed. The villager costumes had the right feel to them and the dance set for Puttin’ on the Ritz were very good, as were the ancestors’ costumes reminiscent of the Addams Family chorus. The principal costumes were

particularly good, with Elizabeth Benning looking classy and luxurious and Inga looking like she stepped out of a seventies soft-porn video. Frau Blúcher was suitably dour looking, and Inspector Kemp was suitably military. Most outstanding was the great outfit worn by The Monster. I just wish he had been given higher-blocked heels to make him that little bit more imposing. There was good attention to wigs and hairstyles, and the make-up team did a good job, especially with the monster.

St. Agnes’ should be delighted to have presented such an enjoyable night of entertainment, which only needed more exaggeration and technically enhanced to give it that extra Wow Factor! Thank you to all concerned for a very pleasurable experience.
reviews.wix_title: Young Frankenstein as presented by St. Agnes Choral Society

reviews.review_text:
Bray Musical Society presented ‘We Will Rock You’ at the Mermaid Arts Centre in Bray against a backdrop of chaos across Dublin, with fuel protests causing major traffic disruption and delays throughout the city. Despite all of that, we made it through the madness and were rewarded with a fun night’s entertainment packed with some of Queen’s most iconic tunes and Ben Elton’s endless stream of puns, jokes and one-liners. It was exactly what we needed that night. Something loud, silly, energetic and over the top. Whatever chaos was happening outside the theatre doors was forgotten for a couple of hours everyone left in very good form.

There was a great buzz in the packed foyer of the Mermaid before the show. The atmosphere was lively and there was a real sense of anticipation in the building. Front of house were dealing with large numbers but everything appeared organised and well managed throughout. Despite the business, patrons were moved through efficiently and the evening ran smoothly. The AIMS President was also in attendance on the night and we were made to feel extremely welcome and very well looked after for what was a very entertaining evening.

Director Chris Currid did very good work with what is quite a difficult show to navigate, at times. There was a good sense throughout that Mr. Currid understood the rhythm of the piece and the importance of momentum. The incorporation of pre-recorded video material was one of the production’s strongest elements. Bringing cast members into the audience during ‘Headlong’ while Heartbreak Hotel was assembled onstage was a very smart piece of direction that kept the pace moving so well. ‘Hammer to Fall’ was another standout sequence. The angry confrontation between Galileo and Scaramouche captured their frustration and emotional exhaustion very well. Comedy was generally handled very well too, which is crucial in this show. There were moments where I felt that the direction could have pushed further. Some principals appeared slightly unsure of the heightened performance style required for this material. Delivery needs to be larger than life and knowing and I felt that not everybody was fully comfortable operating at that pitch all of the time. That aside, this was a confident and well-paced piece of direction overall and there was plenty of imagination evident throughout the evening.

Musical Director Elizabeth Gregan led the band from the pit and there was no question that a great deal of work had gone into the musical preparation. Principal vocals were very strong throughout and it was obvious that careful attention had been given to the show’s wonderful harmonies and choral arrangements. There were moments where that really shone through, particularly in some of the offstage vocals and quieter sections. Unfortunately, however, there were also fairly significant balance issues throughout much of the show and it would be unfair not to mention them. The bass levels were far too dominant for most of the show and, while the bass playing itself was excellent, the overall mix often became so bass-heavy that vocal harmonies and ensemble singing were swallowed up entirely. Whenever the balance settled, harmonies were clear and accurate. The offstage vocals in particular were often beautifully blended, giving a glimpse of the potential that was there.

Roisin Currid’s choreography played a big part in keeping the energy levels high throughout. There was a wide range of ability onstage but the choreography rarely felt beyond anybody’s reach and the overall effect was that movement always looked comfortable and confident. ‘Radio Ga Ga’ was strong, with very good synchronicity throughout and sharp disciplined movement that captured the cold uniformity of the Globalsoft world very well. ‘‘Killer Queen’ was one of the standout routines of the night. The choreography had flair and plenty of attitude, which suited both the character and the music perfectly. ‘Seven Seas of Rhye’ featured some excellent chair choreography that was inventive and very together. ‘Fat Bottomed Girls’ was undoubtedly one of the highlights of the evening. It was unapologetically bold and risqué, exactly as the number needs to be. The girls committed fully to its style and humour and the final picture gave the number a wonderful finish.

Jordan Bass brought great energy to the role of Galileo Figaro. This was a performance full of personality and strong comic instinct. Mr. Bass was extremely animated throughout and made very good use of physicality with his awkward gestures, nervous movement and exaggerated reactions. He judged the tone well as he committed to the madness and humour of the piece. Vocally, he was one of the production’s strongest assets. His singing had great power and he handled the demanding Queen score with confidence. ‘I Want to Break Free’ showed off his range and vocal strength particularly well, while also showing his strong musicality. This musicality was especially evident during ‘Bohemian Rhapsody’, one of the most challenging numbers in the show vocally.

Sophie Walsh brought wonderful presence to the role of Scaramouche. Her dry, sarcastic delivery was brilliantly judged throughout. She had great comic timing and was very comfortable with the style of comedy required. Ms Walsh was a very accomplished singer too. ‘Somebody to Love’ was one of the musical highlights of the production, with great power and control in her voice. ‘Under Pressure’ was another standout moment musically, with Ms. Walsh and Mr. Bass blending beautifully together. Her strongest moment came during ‘Hammer to Fall’. There was a real emotional edge to her performance here as she delivered the anger and frustration of the scene with great vocal and dramatic strength.

Lyndsay Tracey had tremendous stage presence as Killer Queen and fully embraced the outrageous nature of the character. She dominated the stage the moment she appeared with her commanding physicality and sharp delivery. She too had great comic timing and clearly understood the tongue-in-cheek innuendo and sarcasm. Ms. Tracey had an excellent voice. ‘Killer Queen’ suited her very well and allowed her to show off her power and personality. Timing slipped slightly during ‘A Kind of Magic’ but she recovered and kept going like a pro.

A standout performance came from James Scott as Khashoggi, Killer Queen’s sinister right-hand man. Mr. Scott was excellent as an almost comic-book type villain. He brought a very cool, controlled presence to the role but there was always an underlying menace beneath the surface. Vocally, he really came into his own during ‘Seven Seas of Rhye’. There was wonderful authority in his vocal delivery. Much of his humour came through understatement and deadpan delivery and that worked so well against the more exaggerated characters around him. Overall, excellent work from Mr. Scott in what was a most entertaining performance.

Conor Martin gave a solid performance as the rebellious Bohemian, Brit. The character is one of the more exaggerated figures in the show and Mr. Martin brought plenty of enthusiasm and commitment to the role. He was a strong singer, showing great power and range in ‘Headlong’ and ‘I Want It All’. From an acting perspective, there was plenty of potential on display. I did feel, however, that the performance could perhaps have been pushed even further stylistically. ‘We Will Rock You’ exists in a very heightened theatrical world. At times, Mr. Martin seemed slightly restrained and a little more focus on the role’s comic absurdity might have made what was a strong performance even better.

Tia Tyndall-Kenna did well in the role of Oz. Ms. Tyndall-Kenna brought plenty of attitude and presence to the role, particularly in the musical numbers. She was at her strongest vocally, with some superb singing, most notably during ‘I Want It All’, where her riffing and vocal control were extremely impressive. The quality of her voice was excellent. At times, though, I found myself wanting her to fully let go and trust just how good she actually was. The vocal ability was absolutely there, but there were moments where the performance felt slightly held back when it could perhaps have exploded even further with confidence and attitude.

Eoin Martin played Buddy as a laid-back, ageing hippie type, with a very relaxed delivery throughout. There was something very likeable about the performance. Buddy is a character who should drive the comedy directly at the audience. Mr. Martin occasionally seemed a little hesitant in that regard. The opportunities were there for him to really eyeball the audience, own the room and embrace the madness of the material but at times it felt like he was gently tapping the fourth wall rather than breaking it. Mr. Martin was another very strong singer. ‘These Are the Days of Our Lives’ was beautifully sincere and, despite the sound balance issues affecting the number, he still impressed vocally. With a little more confidence in pushing the character’s theatricality and audience interaction further, it could have been a truly standout portrayal.

Ruth Coughlan made a very strong impression in the cameo role of Teacher and showed herself to be an excellent character actress. She fully committed to the heightened style of the show from the moment she appeared and brought great energy and confidence to the role.

The ensemble was very committed throughout. Whether appearing as Bohemians, Yuppies, Ga Ga Kids or Fat Bottomed Girls, there was a very strong sense that they had bought into the madcap tone of the production and that they were enjoying every minute. Kudos to the production team for instilling this in their cast. The Bohemians in particular brought great life to the stage. There was a lovely sense of interplay and casual banter between them that made the group feel like a believable community. A lot of work had obviously gone into the vocal preparation of the ensemble. The rich harmonies were there and whenever the sound balance settled, the quality was very apparent. Performance levels during the choreographed sections were consistently high, with the cast maintaining strong energy and commitment right across the evening.

The set design was functional and versatile, giving the cast plenty of space to work with in the large open playing area. The large upstage platform was used to very good effect, creating opportunities for levels and varied staging. The central stair unit was another useful element. Much of the atmosphere came from the LED screens which did a lot of the heavy lifting visually. The graphics and pre-recorded video material were extremely well created and gave the production a very polished look. The futuristic imagery, animated backgrounds and filmed inserts added much excitement and humour to scenes. Overall, the combination of staging, graphics and video content worked very well together to create a practical playing space which offered great versatility and fluidity for the production team.

Gerry McCann’s stage management was excellent throughout and the show ran with impressive smoothness from a technical point of view. The crew were extremely slick and well-rehearsed, carrying out all scene changes with speed and efficiency and maintaining great pace and momentum through the show. While ‘We Will Rock You’ does not rely on large-scale moving scenery to the same extent as some productions, there was still plenty happening behind the scenes and everything appeared highly organised.

The lighting design played a huge role in creating atmosphere throughout the show. There was a strong understanding of the rock-concert aesthetic of ‘We Will Rock You’, while still maintaining the atmospheric moments required in musical theatre. The use of side lighting was particularly effective, combined with haze and strong colour choices. ‘Under Pressure’ was especially well handled. The cueing here was excellent, with a very effective blend of musical theatre precision and rock-gig atmosphere which helped to heighten the tension and connection between Galileo and Scaramouche. ‘No One But You’ was another standout moment with lighting allowing the emotion of the song to come through naturally. ‘Seven Seas of Rhye’ featured some very clever design and cueing choices as the Bohemians were ‘processed’. One of the upstage lighting bars appeared to bounce at various points during the show and this had a knock on with lights moving erratically on the stage at times. The distraction wasn’t a major one but it did draw the eye.

Sound was probably the area of the production that most needed attention on the night. I don’t know whether some of the issues stemmed from limitations within the house PA itself, but I can only respond to what was heard on the night and unfortunately there were some fairly significant balance problems throughout the show. The main issue was the dominance of the bass within the overall mix. At times it was overpowering to the point that vocals were being lost underneath it. ‘These Are the Days of Our Lives’ was probably the moment where the issue became most noticeable. Because it is a softer, more reflective number, the heavy bass presence underneath it was even more apparent and, unfortunately, took away from the number’s warmth. There was also plenty of evidence of how good the sound design could be when the balance sat properly. Offstage vocals were often beautifully amplified and blended. ‘I Want It All’ sounded excellent, while the offstage vocals during ‘Headlong’ were particularly strong and showed the quality of the choral work very well. Dialogue throughout the show was very clear. Principals were, for the most part, well supported vocally and cueing for dialogue was excellent throughout. Sound effects were also well chosen and very well timed.

Costumes were one of the production’s strongest elements. There was a very good understanding throughout of the contrast between the conformity of Globalsoft and the chaos of the Bohemians. The Bohemians looked excellent as a group. There was tartan, leather, mesh, chains, distressed fabrics and mismatched accessories everywhere. Oz’s punk-inspired styling and Brit’s tartan-heavy look were excellent. The Globalsoft aesthetic worked very well too, especially the ensemble’s silver, white and metallic uniforms. Killer Queen was especially successful with her bold red palette ensuring she dominated the stage whenever she appeared. Khashoggi’s long black coat and sharp tailoring gave him an imposing presence which suited the character perfectly. Buddy’s tie-dye colours and headband brought great visual humour to the character. The ensemble overall were extremely well dressed throughout. Excellent work throughout.

Hair and makeup complemented the costume design very effectively. Strong eye makeup, textured hairstyles, wigs, braids and metallic styling all contributed to the overall visual. Killer Queen’s bold makeup and vivid red hair were particularly striking, while Buddy’s wig and ageing were nice details.

There was very good work from the props department throughout, with plenty of attention paid to the quirky, offbeat nature of the show. Brit’s homemade instrument was excellent. It genuinely looked cobbled together out of scraps and random materials. The ‘cattle prods’ used during the ‘processing’ of the Bohemians were also very effective. Small details like Killer Queen’s whip were very effective and the Harley during ‘Headlong’ gave the scene a real injection of energy and attitude when it appeared onstage. The all-important videotape was another key part of the story. Overall, there was excellent attention to detail from the props team throughout.

‘We Will Rock You’ is one of those shows that needs energy, commitment and a group willing to unapologetically throw itself into the madness of its world. Bray Musical Society certainly did that. We were left with the sense of a society which had given absolutely everything to the show. There was great ambition, creativity and heart throughout. In the midst of a chaotic evening outside the theatre, Bray Musical Society succeeded in doing exactly what theatre is supposed to do; it transported its audience somewhere else for a few hours and sent us home smiling. Job done.
reviews.wix_title: Review: We Will Rock You - Bray Musical Society

reviews.review_text:
Brief Overview of Show and Evaluation of Front of House

Pop Up Theatre’s production of Sweeney Todd was an ambitious, inventive, and atmospheric retelling of Sondheim’s notoriously complex musical thriller. From the moment one entered the venue, it was clear that this would be an immersive theatrical experience. The creative team made strong, brave choices in their approach to both staging and audience engagement, and although not all of them landed perfectly, the overall tone was one of dedication and creative exploration. It’s no small task to tackle a piece as musically intricate and emotionally intense as Sweeney Todd , but the company leaned in with enthusiasm, a clear aesthetic, and genuine dramatic intention.

The Front of House team were courteous, efficient, and welcoming. Their warmth and professionalism helped set a relaxed and anticipatory atmosphere before the curtain rose. While the unusual staging meant some audience members had slightly compromised views, staff did their best to assist, and the general buzz and excitement added to the show's immersive quality.

Director – Direction and Production

Karen Gordon’s vision for this production was bold and inspired. Her decision to stage the piece in thrust formation, with actors weaving in and out of the audience, created a sense of claustrophobia and tension that was very fitting for the grim tale. This layout invited the audience into the grimy alleys and haunted parlours of Fleet Street, which was an effective atmospheric choice. Some of the spatial elements, however, posed challenges, particularly for audience members seated in areas with less direct sightlines. While immersive theatre is thrilling, it must balance innovation with accessibility.

The overall concept was cohesive and thoughtful. There were several moments of visual and dramatic brilliance, particularly the fluidity of movement between audience and performance space, and the imaginative staging of ensemble scenes. However, more care was needed in maintaining the internal logic of the world being built. For instance, some costume pairings blurred class boundaries in ways that felt unintentional and confusing. Character dynamics, such as high society women walking arm in arm with their maids, or prostitutes, compromised the class structure that is so integral to the plot’s tension.

Characterisation was another area that could have benefited from deeper exploration. Sweeney and Mrs. Lovett, while played with commitment, seemed emotionally static. These are characters with rich internal lives and a gradual descent (or ascent) into madness, and the lack of a visible arc diluted the show’s dramatic payoff. That said, other characters showed clear development and careful crafting, and there was evidence of a director who had a clear grasp of the show’s tone and themes.

Musical Director – Direction and Orchestra

The musical direction under Niamh Crowley was one of the highlights of the production. The orchestral sound was full-bodied, lush, and perfectly suited to Sondheim’s haunting score. Particularly impressive was the handling of complex rhythmic patterns and tonal dissonances, elements which often trip up even the most seasoned performers. The musicians were tightly unified, and the transitions between tempos and dynamics were seamless.

It was remarkable to observe such flawless cuing, especially considering the positioning of the MD, who was placed side-stage, largely hidden from both cast and chorus. Despite this, entrances were crisp, exits were clean, and the ensemble never lost tempo or cohesion. This speaks to the clarity of rehearsal, the strength of direction, and the trust between musical leader and cast.

There were occasional issues with tuning and diction among some principals. In a show as lyrically intricate as Sweeney Todd , the intelligibility of lyrics is crucial to both narrative clarity and audience engagement. These minor setbacks, however, did not detract significantly from the overall musical quality, which remained a major strength throughout.

Choreographer – Choreography

Ciara Frahill brought fresh, intelligent movement to the production, particularly evident in the opening number, which was a dynamic and visually striking piece of storytelling. The choreography was modern and expressive without feeling anachronistic. It supported rather than distracted from the mood, and it cleverly echoed the unease and urgency of the score.

Ciara’s use of spatial awareness and movement across the thrust stage was particularly effective. The ensemble work flowed beautifully, with natural transitions and well-defined formations that enhanced the chaotic yet controlled energy of the narrative. The choreography felt organic to the world, never inserted for spectacle alone, and that grounding added a great deal of authenticity.

There is always room for tightening in such large-scale movement pieces, but the commitment of the cast ensured that any small moments of looseness were quickly covered with energy and intent.

Leading Principals – Singing and Acting

Sweeney Todd – Dave Flynn: Dave’s Sweeney had presence and vocal depth, but greater attention to diction and character development was needed to bring the role fully to life. The menace required for the role never quite landed, and a broader emotional range, particularly the descent into madness, was not fully explored. As a result, Sweeney’s journey felt more linear than layered.

Mrs. Lovett – Hazel Doolan: Hazel approached the role with confidence, but more vocal support and emotional shading were needed. Mrs. Lovett’s complexity, her wit, desperation, and eventual unraveling, requires more variety in both vocal and physical choices. The performance stayed on one emotional level for much of the show, which limited its impact.

Judge Turpin – Hugh O’Neill: Hugh’s portrayal was unsettling and physically imposing, in line with the character’s sinister nature. A little more focus on vocal clarity and accent consistency would elevate the performance even further.

Anthony Hope – Jack Courtenay: Jack’s Anthony was sincere and likable, though his portrayal occasionally lacked assertiveness. This character often serves as the moral compass of the piece, and more vocal strength and emotional conviction would help anchor that role more effectively.

Beggar Woman – Aoife Kelly: An absolute standout, Aoife delivered a nuanced, layered, and physically committed performance. Her characterisation was rich with detail, each twitch, mutter, and flicker of recognition added depth. Her facial expressions and vocal inflections made the mystery and tragedy of the Beggar Woman vividly clear.

Beadle Bamford – Kieran Cunnane: Kieran leaned fearlessly into the grotesque. His performance was both chilling and darkly humorous, with excellent use of body language and a consistent, disturbing accent. One of the most memorable portrayals in the production.

Supporting Roles – Singing and Acting

Johanna – Katelyn Rafter: Katelyn presented a poised and engaging Johanna. Her stage presence was graceful, and she handled the role’s demands with ease. Some additional layering in her emotional beats would enhance the character’s inner conflict.

Tobias Ragg – Niall Kerr: Niall’s Tobias was charming, naïve, and loveable. His performance was heartfelt and honest, and his vocal tone suited the role well. A sensitive and endearing portrayal.

Adolfo Pirelli – Conor White: Conor was a joy to watch. His flamboyant physicality and vocal energy made Pirelli a delightfully theatrical character. The switch in accents was flawlessly executed and added comic sharpness to the role.

Mr. Fogg – Maurice Kehoe: Maurice gave a strong and appropriately unhinged performance. His scene was brief but impactful, showing clear character commitment and vocal authority.

Chorus/Ensemble – Singing, Acting and Choreography

The ensemble in this production was a clear asset. Their commitment to the world of the piece was unwavering, and each performer brought individual characterisation, ensuring that the crowd scenes felt alive and textured. Their vocal sound was balanced, strong, and well-rehearsed, an impressive feat considering the complexity of the choral arrangements.

Their movement across the stage was polished and thoughtful, creating dynamic pictures while supporting the leads. This was an ensemble that understood its role as both storyteller and atmospheric backdrop, and the synergy among them elevated the entire production.

Stage Management & Set Design

The set design was functional and effective, utilising the venue’s thrust configuration to create a fluid, immersive environment. The use of house facades on either end of the hall was a clever touch, enhancing the sense of place for audience members seated at the sides.

Minimal stage management was needed, as furniture shifts were integrated smoothly into the action by the cast. This approach supported the piece’s momentum and tone without pulling focus. Overall, it was a smart and efficient use of resources that served the production well.

Technical – Lighting and Sound

Lighting was a triumph in this production. Moody, atmospheric, and beautifully tailored to each scene, it underscored the narrative with precision. Shadows were used to great effect, heightening tension and mystery, and the cueing was sharp and reliable. Spot work was impressively accurate, which is not easy in a thrust setting.

Sound design, while mostly excellent, faced a few physical limitations due to the venue’s layout. The mix itself was well-balanced, and voices were generally clear and distinct. However, depending on where one sat, some speakers were angled away from the audience, which occasionally affected the directionality of the sound. Nonetheless, the quality of the overall mix and the interplay between vocals, orchestra, and choir was strong.

Visual – Costumes, Hair and Make-Up

Costumes were largely appropriate and well-executed. In immersive theatre, detail becomes paramount, and small things, such as visible safety pins or improperly fastened gowns, can distract from the costume plot. Closer detail to costume decisions, when casts have made character choices, is needed. This will help avoid clashes in social strata.

Hair and make-up were particularly strong. Hairstyles were consistent with the era and enhanced each character’s presence. The make-up was atmospheric and appropriate. The Beggar Woman could have pushed further into transformative territory to heighten the dramatic irony of Sweeney not recognising his beloved wife.

Adjudicator’s Suggestions / Overall Comments

Pop Up Theatre should be proud of what they achieved with this production. Tackling Sweeney Todd is no small feat, and the overall concept, commitment of the cast, and strong creative vision made for an enjoyable and often haunting evening of theatre.

Moving forward, refining diction and vocal technique among the leads will greatly enhance narrative clarity. Ensuring the design elements, particularly costume and staging, work together to support the story’s internal logic will help preserve immersion. And continuing to explore the emotional arcs of major characters will add depth and impact to key moments.

This was an imaginative and courageous production, filled with promise and passion. With continued focus on detail and cohesion, this company is capable of producing truly unforgettable work.
reviews.wix_title: Sweeney Todd as presented by Pop-up Theatre

reviews.review_text:
St. Mary’s Choral Society presented a warm, heartfelt, and visually enchanting production of The Clockmaker’s Daughter, capturing the whimsical spirit and emotional sincerity of this beautiful musical with great care and affection. From the opening moments, the audience was drawn into a world that felt both magical and intimate, filled with warmth, humanity, and strong storytelling.

Director Des Henn guided the production with a clear understanding of the heart of the piece, allowing the emotional narrative to unfold naturally while maintaining a lovely pace and energy throughout. The storytelling was handled thoughtfully, with quieter moments given time to breathe while still sustaining momentum. Relationships between characters felt believable and lived-in, helping to create a convincing sense of community within the village setting. The production balanced comedy and emotion particularly well. The humour never felt forced, instead emerging naturally from character interactions and situations. Scenes involving Ma Riley brought genuine warmth and laughter to the performance, providing welcome moments of levity that complemented the more emotional aspects of the story beautifully. There was a strong emotional clarity throughout much of the production, particularly in the central relationship between Constance and Will. Their connection developed with tenderness and honesty, giving the audience a relationship they could fully invest in. The wider ensemble also contributed enormously to the authenticity of the world being created onstage, with many characters feeling fully fleshed out and grounded within the village community. At times, some aspects of the physical storytelling around the set could perhaps have been defined with slightly more precision, particularly around the stream and bridge area, where distinctions between water and land occasionally became a little blurred. However, these moments were minor within an otherwise cohesive production and could easily be refined further in future performances.

One particularly interesting aspect of the direction was Constance’s journey from automaton to human. The initial physicality established her mechanical nature very effectively, immediately creating a sense of “otherness.” As the production progressed, there may have been room to allow that physical transformation to unfold even more gradually, heightening the emotional impact of her development. Nonetheless, the concept was clearly considered and remained engaging throughout. Accent work across the production leaned toward a broad Irish sound rather than a clearly defined regional dialect. While consistency varied slightly, the warmth and sincerity of the performances ensured the charm of the production remained fully intact.

Musically, the production was exceptionally strong. Niall Kelly’s musical direction was a major asset to the evening, with the orchestra delivering a lush and emotionally rich interpretation of the score. The flowing melodies were handled beautifully, while the more rhythmic sections maintained strong drive and energy throughout. Tempos were extremely well judged, supporting both the pacing of the storytelling and the emotional atmosphere of the piece. The positioning of the orchestra was also a particularly effective choice. Having the musicians facing stage right, with the standing Musical Director positioned to the side, ensured the audience maintained clear sightlines to the stage while still allowing excellent communication between cast and pit. It was an inventive staging solution that worked well within the venue. Vocally, the production was outstanding. The ensemble harmonies were rich, balanced, and beautifully blended, creating a glorious choral sound throughout the evening. The opening and closing numbers were especially moving, filled with emotional phrasing and excellent clarity of diction. Entrances and cut-offs remained consistently secure, demonstrating the strength of rehearsal preparation and musical discipline across the company.

Barbara Meany’s choreography worked extremely effectively within what was clearly a limited stage space. Rather than overcrowding the stage, the movement remained purposeful, character-driven, and visually engaging throughout. Changing formations were used cleverly to maintain visual interest, while the choreography itself complemented the intimate nature of the musical beautifully. “Raise A Glass” stood out in particular as a wonderfully energetic and entertaining number. The cast performed it with enthusiasm and confidence, creating a lovely sense of celebration and community. Throughout the production, the ensemble appeared comfortable and well-rehearsed in the movement, contributing significantly to the warmth and vitality of the show.

Saoirse Scully delivered a beautifully sincere and emotionally engaging performance as Constance. Vocally, she was strong, singing with maturity, sensitivity, and a lovely emotional nuance that suited the score. Her portrayal captured Constance’s innocence and fascination with the world beautifully. There was a wide-eyed curiosity to the performance that made the character immediately endearing. Her initial mechanical physicality was particularly effective and clearly established the character’s unique nature from the outset. As the production progressed, the transition toward more human movement perhaps developed a touch quicker than expected, though the emotional honesty of the performance ensured the audience remained fully invested throughout. Her scenes with Emmett Donlan’s Will were especially touching. The chemistry between the pair felt entirely natural and believable, and together they created the emotional heart of the production.

Emmett Donlan gave a wonderfully gentle and sincere performance as Will Riley. He brought an effortless warmth and authenticity to the role, creating a character that felt grounded, kind, and emotionally open. Vocally, he was superb, with a tenor voice that soared beautifully through the score while maintaining clarity, sincerity, and emotional connection. There was a lovely softness and vulnerability to his acting that suited the role perfectly. He appeared completely at ease onstage, allowing the audience to connect instantly with the character. His vocal blend with Saoirse Scully was particularly beautiful, and together they elevated many of the show’s key emotional moments.

James O’Donovan delivered a thoughtful and emotionally layered portrayal of Abraham Reed. He effectively conveyed the internal conflict of a man struggling with pride, fear, responsibility, and emotional attachment. At times the performance leaned more heavily toward frustration and anger, though there were also some lovely glimpses of vulnerability that added further depth to the character. Vocally, he performed strongly throughout the evening, with “You’re Still Here” proving particularly moving and emotionally sincere.

Sheena Fennessy brought tremendous humour and personality to the role of Ma Riley. Her portrayal captured the recognisable qualities of a classic Irish matriarch well, and her comic timing generated many genuine laughs throughout the evening. Her transitions between irritation, warmth, nosiness, and hospitality were handled naturally, particularly when realising there may be financial gain involved in the situation. Vocally, some of the higher material appeared slightly outside her most comfortable range, but this was more than compensated for through strong characterisation and expressive storytelling. Her emotional turn following her shooting of Will was especially well handled and brought an added layer of humanity to the character.

Nicole Butler and Cormac Maher were extremely charming as Amelia Kelly and Henry Glynn. Their chemistry felt natural and relaxed, and they brought humour and warmth to the wedding dress storyline without ever overplaying it. Vocally, both blended beautifully with one another and with the wider ensemble. Cian Corcoran brought a gentle warmth to Mayor Glynn and contributed nicely to the atmosphere of the village community. While there were moments where additional vocal confidence would further strengthen the performance, the sincerity and commitment of the portrayal remained evident throughout.

The group of seamstresses, Rhiannon – Eabha Morrissey, Moll – Rachel Browne, Cara – Aoibhe Condon, Jane – Nicole Kennedy, Mary – Siobhan Scanlon, and Lucille – Aine Purcell, worked wonderfully together as a unit. Their gossiping was particularly entertaining, filled with expressive reactions while remaining grounded within the world of the piece. Vocally, they blended extremely well and consistently enhanced the texture of the ensemble numbers. Featured ensemble members, Mab – Gillian Scully, Sam – Nathan Dalton, and Mr. Reed – George Barry, all contributed strongly, remaining focused and engaged throughout while integrating seamlessly into the wider company.

Indeed, the ensemble as a whole was one of the greatest strengths of the production. Their singing throughout the evening was stunning, producing rich harmonies and an exceptionally well blended sound. The opening and closing numbers were especially moving, creating powerful emotional moments through the strength of the ensemble vocals. Acting within the ensemble was equally strong. Every performer appeared fully invested in the storytelling, helping to create a believable and fully realised stage world. Background interactions remained engaged and authentic throughout, while the choreography was performed confidently and with ease.

Visually, the production was absolutely beautiful. The set design demonstrated enormous attention to detail and perfectly complemented the whimsical, fairytale atmosphere of the piece. The downstage houses that opened to reveal Abraham’s workshop and Ma Riley’s shop were particularly effective, while the hidden access doors built into the set, for the stage crew to rearrange the internal decor, reflected a very impressive level of technical thought and craftsmanship. The moving bridge also worked extremely well, enhancing both the storytelling and the physical environment of the show.

Jimmy Trehy’s stage management was excellent throughout. Scene changes were executed swiftly and smoothly, ensuring the production maintained momentum even during larger transitions.

Lighting and sound were both of an extremely high standard. The lighting design created several genuinely beautiful stage pictures, particularly during solo moments where mood and atmosphere were enhanced very effectively. The moon projected onto the back wall was a lovely touch, while the fairy lights woven across the stage through branches and rooftops created an utterly magical atmosphere for Will’s special place. Sound quality remained consistently polished throughout the evening. The balance between orchestra and vocals was excellent, particularly important in the intimate venue, and individual vocals were always clear and well supported.

Costumes, hair, and makeup all complemented the production beautifully. The costume palette worked wonderfully alongside the set design, while the styling remained thoughtful and appropriate to the world of the show. Hair and makeup were neat, effective, and suitably period appropriate without becoming distracting.

Front of house operations also contributed positively to the overall experience. The audience was welcomed warmly on arrival, and the organisation throughout the venue helped create a lovely atmosphere of anticipation before the performance even began. There was a clear sense of pride within the society that extended beyond the stage and into the overall audience experience.

Overall, St. Mary’s Choral Society delivered a heartfelt, visually stunning, and musically accomplished production of The Clockmaker’s Daughter. The warmth and sincerity at the centre of the performance ensured the audience remained emotionally invested throughout, while the strength of the ensemble, the beauty of the score, and the detailed visual presentation combined to create a truly memorable evening of theatre. The company should be extremely proud of what they achieved with this production.
reviews.wix_title: Review: The Clockmaker’s Daughter - St. Mary’s Choral Society

reviews.review_text:
Gorey Musical Society took on the hugely ambitious The Hunchback of Notre Dame with confidence, imagination, and an impressive understanding of the emotional depth required to make the piece work. It is a musical that demands enormous vocal power, strong visual storytelling, and an ability to balance darkness with moments of genuine warmth and humanity. This production succeeded in doing exactly that, delivering an evening that was musically thrilling, visually striking, and emotionally engaging throughout.

Under Megan Lopez’s direction, the show maintained a strong sense of flow and momentum from beginning to end. The storytelling was consistently clear, even during the larger ensemble scenes, and the integration of the storytellers into the action worked especially well. Their movement in and out of scenes felt seamless, adding continuity and helping the narrative move naturally from one moment to the next. The overall visual identity of the production was cohesive and thoughtful, with a strong understanding of the gothic atmosphere at the heart of the piece. The use of the statues and gargoyles as part of the storytelling framework was particularly effective. Having them preset within the arches as the audience entered immediately established the world of the cathedral and created a wonderful moment of surprise when they later came to life. Lopez handled tonal shifts with confidence, allowing the darker moments of the story to land while still leaving space for tenderness and emotional connection. The final image of Quasimodo’s parents returning as spirits to welcome him at the end of the show was especially moving and provided a beautiful sense of full-circle closure. There were a few areas where the storytelling could have been pushed even further. The physical violence between Frollo and Esmeralda somewhat lacked the intensity needed to fully justify the emotional reaction that followed, and some additional use of the upper levels during larger crowd scenes may have added greater visual depth. Similarly, while the decision to largely retain Irish accents throughout the production was an interesting choice, the contrast with Frollo’s more traditionally “villainous” English accent sometimes felt stylistically inconsistent.

Musically, however, this was an outstanding production. Conor McCarthy’s musical direction was exceptional and formed the backbone of the evening. From the opening moments, the orchestra created a rich and ethereal soundscape that perfectly suited the grandeur of the score. The balance between pit and performers was superb throughout, particularly impressive given the size of the orchestra. Individual instrumental lines remained crystal clear, while vocal harmonies were never lost beneath the orchestration. The chorus and choir work was especially breathtaking. Harmonies were precise and beautifully controlled, with the dissonant sections delivered confidently and cleanly. The closing moments of the opening number were genuinely thrilling, filling the auditorium with a sound that felt almost physical in its impact. The ensemble singing throughout the evening was consistently powerful, and the discipline of the choir was remarkable considering many performers were positioned upstage or behind principal action for large sections of the show. Transitions between dialogue and music were also handled beautifully, with underscoring flowing naturally into songs and maintaining emotional momentum throughout. Principal vocals were consistently strong, although diction occasionally became unclear in some of the larger or more intense vocal passages. Nonetheless, the overall musical standard of the production was extremely high.

Megan Lopez’s choreography complemented the production very effectively. Rather than attempting movement beyond the cast’s abilities, the choreography embraced their strengths and created visually engaging moments that always served the storytelling. The armography throughout the show was particularly effective, creating strong stage pictures and adding fluidity to ensemble scenes. The use of scarves during “Topsy Turvy” worked especially well, bringing colour, movement, and texture to the stage, while the circular formations suited the period aesthetic beautifully. Importantly, everyone on stage always appeared involved and connected to the action, creating a strong sense of ensemble cohesion.

Andrew O’Grady delivered a warm and emotionally sincere performance as Quasimodo. One of the strongest elements of his portrayal was the distinction he created between Quasimodo’s inner world and the way he presented himself to the outside world. His scenes with the gargoyles felt freer and more natural, while his physicality shifted during interactions with the citizens of Paris. There was perhaps room to explore the physical contrast between those two states even further, but the emotional honesty of the performance ensured the audience remained deeply invested in him throughout. Vocally, he sang with apparent ease and genuine emotional connection, particularly in his scenes with Esmeralda, which carried real warmth and tenderness.

Margaret Masterson gave a commanding and confident performance as Esmeralda. She brought enormous strength and determination to the role, creating a character who was proud, defensive, and fiercely independent. Vocally, the role sat very comfortably within her range, and she handled the demanding score with confidence and control. At times, it would have been interesting to see a little more vulnerability emerge within quieter moments, particularly in her relationship with Quasimodo, as occasionally the intensity remained level throughout. However, this was still a committed and engaging portrayal.

Rónán P. Byrne delivered one of the standout performances of the evening as Frollo. He captured the character’s duality exceptionally well, balancing outward piety and authority with the inner torment and obsession consuming him beneath the surface. His transition from younger to older Frollo was subtle and believable, achieved through carefully judged changes in both physicality and vocal tone. Vocally, he possessed a rich and mature sound that suited the role beautifully, and “Hellfire” became one of the undeniable highlights of the production. The number was dramatically gripping and vocally commanding, elevated further by striking technical elements including the projection of a stained-glass window shattering gradually throughout the scene, mirroring Frollo’s psychological collapse.

Richard O’Toole brought warmth and complexity to Phoebus, successfully balancing the character’s swagger and confidence with glimpses of the emotional trauma beneath the surface. His first entrance hinted briefly at the scars left by war and immediately gave the character greater depth. His growing love for Esmeralda and gradual questioning of his own belief system were communicated clearly throughout the performance. Vocally, he blended particularly well with Esmerelda during their shared material.

Among the supporting cast, Tommy Cox brought strong energy and fluid physicality to Clopin, with a movement style that suited the role beautifully. At times he slightly anticipated reactions physically before delivering lines, but overall, he remained an engaging and charismatic presence. Brian Cooney and Megan Mitten both gave convincing performances as Jehan Frollo and Florika respectively, with Jehan’s death scene proving particularly realistic. Justin Grimes integrated seamlessly into the statue ensemble as Saint Aphrodisius, while Rónán Ó Dubhghaill and Maria Forrest contributed strongly in their featured ensemble roles.

The gargoyles and statues were a major strength of the production. John Donohoe, Becky Sillery Murphy, Paul Kehoe, and Shauna Crooke worked exceptionally well as a group, maintaining strong ensemble chemistry while still allowing individual personalities to emerge. Their physicality and facial expressions remained clear and expressive despite the extensive makeup, and vocally they blended beautifully together. The storytellers also played a crucial role in maintaining the momentum of the production. Thomas Rush, April Kelly, Niamh Flemming, Melissa Larkin, Caoimhe Boyle, and Ciara Herron brought excellent energy and clarity to the narrative, moving fluidly in and out of scenes and helping sustain the pace of the show throughout.

The ensemble as a whole was outstanding. Vocally, the chorus produced a rich and powerful sound that repeatedly raised goosebumps, adding enormous emotional weight to many of the production’s biggest moments. Beyond the singing, the ensemble remained consistently engaged and invested in the storytelling, with every performer appearing fully committed to the world of the piece.

Visually, the production was equally strong. The set design created an effective framework for the storytelling, with the lighter stone-inspired palette beautifully reflecting the architecture and atmosphere of the cathedral. The asymmetrical staging, featuring a staircase on only one side, added visual interest and prevented stage pictures from feeling static. Additional moving set pieces helped transitions flow smoothly, while the projection work during “Hellfire” added another memorable visual layer to the production.

Lighting throughout the show was particularly effective, especially in creating the interior world of the cathedral. The sense of scale and gothic atmosphere was beautifully achieved through careful use of focus, shadow, and colour. The lighting palette complemented the production’s visual identity very well, balancing warmth with darker dramatic moments.

Costumes, hair, and makeup were all of a very high standard. The vibrant gypsy costumes contrasted beautifully against the more muted cathedral tones, while the gargoyle makeup, particularly the green patina detailing on the faces and headpieces, looked excellent. Hair and makeup were consistently period appropriate, with only one small oversight where one gargoyle’s hands had not been painted to match the rest of the design.

Front of House operations were warm, welcoming, and efficiently managed. Audience members were greeted professionally and seated smoothly, helping to create a positive atmosphere before the performance began. There was a genuine sense of excitement in the auditorium, and the company should be commended for maintaining such a polished audience experience throughout the evening.

Overall, Gorey Musical Society delivered a richly atmospheric and emotionally compelling production of The Hunchback of Notre Dame. With stunning musical direction, strong ensemble storytelling, imaginative visuals, and several standout performances, this was a production full of ambition, heart, and theatrical flair that left a lasting impression.

reviews.review_text:
With high expectations, I entered the historic building, eager to see what this production had in store. The audience's anticipation and the buzz in the air were a testament to the society's reputation and the high quality of their productions. This beautiful building entranced me, called The Abbey, which this Society calls home.

The Front of House team's outstanding management skills enabled them to handle the packed houses attracted by the production very easily. They were swift, efficient, and courteous, ensuring that every audience member was seated and ready to enjoy the show in no time at all. Greeting everyone with a smile to make us all feel welcome and at ease. The team took great pride in their work and genuinely cared about the audience's experience. I was already looking forward to the evening!

The Director was Jennifer O’Brien. This young lady is a true visionary, bringing a unique perspective to the show, which is evident in every aspect of the production, from the set design to the costumes. Ms O’Brien’s attention to detail was unparalleled, ensuring that every scene flowed seamlessly into the next, with a remarkable ability to bring out the best in the cast, resulting in beautiful performances. The clear vision for the show was evident in the set design, a visual feast for the eyes. The lighting design was also expertly executed, and the costume work was impressive, with each character's outfit perfectly capturing their personality. Overall, the direction of this show was professional with the characters direction on stage being fabulous. A true sign of hours of individual work with principals especially. Ms O’Brien deserves high praise for her talent in all areas of this lovely production.

The choreographer was Grace McGrath. A true master of her craft. The choreography was complex and challenging, yet the dancers executed every move precisely and gracefully. Every dance routine, perfectly synchronised and expertly executed. The choreography captivated the audience with the dancers' movements, which was all the more impressive given the small stage and backstage restrictions I saw with my own eyes. This production had very little space on or off stage, plus a jam-packed house. What Ms McGrath created here and what the performers did was remarkable.
